candidate_title: XSS via unvalidated wiki-syntax attribute names in XHTML/HTML rendering (element-sanitizer bypass)
candidate_root_cause: XHTMLWikiPrinter.cleanAttributes(...) takes every attribute name rejected by HTMLElementSanitizer.isAttributeAllowed(...) and re-emits it as TRANSLATED_ATTRIBUTE_PREFIX + name without checking that the name is a valid XML/HTML attribute name or escaping it. The resulting map key is used as the SAX attribute qName (XMLWikiPrinter.createAttributes / printXMLStartElement) and the dom4j-based writer only escapes attribute values (XHTMLWriter.escapeAttributeEntities), so the name reaches the browser verbatim. Parameter names are not XML-name constrained on input: WikiScannerUtil.getNextToken treats a quoted token as a whole key (spaces, quotes, '<', '>', '=' allowed) and splitToPairs trims but does not otherwise restrict it, so wiki-syntax link/image/format parameters can carry an attribute name that breaks out of the name position. Attribute values are escaped, so the injection is in the name, and it is never neutralized on output.
candidate_impact: Stored (and, for previews/reflected rendering, reflected) XSS in pages rendered by XWiki Rendering: injected markup or event-handler attributes execute JavaScript in the browser of any user viewing the page, and the HTML element/attribute sanitizer added to block exactly such attributes is bypassed. In deployments where this sanitizer is the only barrier against script execution by non-privileged content editors, the injection crosses the intended privilege boundary (e.g. content that must be inert is rendered as executable HTML).

candidate_root_cause: The realm-scoped admin REST resource classes rely on explicit per-method RealmAuth calls for authorization (auth.requireManage()/requireView()/requireAny()). With a known session id an attacker can forcibly terminate another user's SSO session (including administrators') and trigger application-side logout propagation - a denial of service / session-disruption primitive that persists until re-authentication. The same root cause exposes non-public client metadata (all OAuth client ids of the realm) to any authenticated user, aiding follow-on attacks (e.g., identifying public clients for direct-grant/refresh abuse). candidate_title: Default interpolation lookups expose script evaluation, URL fetch and DNS resolution to interpolation input
candidate_root_cause: DefaultStringLookup enumerates DNS, SCRIPT and URL among the default lookups, and StringLookupFactory.addDefaultStringLookups() installs every enum entry into the prefix dispatch map. InterpolatorStringLookup's default constructor enables all of these lookups, and StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator() builds a substitutor over that singleton. Consequently a template substring such as ${script:javascript:...} is dispatched to ScriptStringLookup, which passes the engine name and script body straight from the variable key to ScriptEngineManager.getEngineByName(...).eval(...) with no validation or allow-list. ${url:...} reaches UrlStringLookup's URL.openStream() and ${dns:...} reaches InetAddress.getByName(). The dangerous lookups are therefore active with zero configuration in a documented public helper.

The vulnerability is in a library helper that is explicitly documented for placeholder substitution (StringSubstitutor.java:288-305), so affected callers commonly process externally supplied template text.

candidate_title: Pre-auth arbitrary class instantiation via OpenWire throwable unmarshalling (createThrowable)
candidate_root_cause: BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable() takes the throwable class name and message directly from the OpenWire byte stream and executes Class.forName(className, false, loader), clazz.getConstructor(String.class) and constructor.newInstance(message) without verifying Throwable.class.isAssignableFrom(clazz) and without any allow-list. The returned object is cast to Throwable only after the constructor call, so a non-Throwable gadget class still runs its constructor/static initialization and the resulting ClassCastException is silently swallowed by the catch (Throwable e) branch. The same duplicated sink exists in every wire-format version (activemq-client v1..v10 and activemq-openwire-legacy v2..v8), and is invoked for the Throwable fields of ExceptionResponse, ConnectionError and MessageAck.poisonCause via tightUnmarsalThrowable/looseUnmarsalThrowable.
candidate_impact: Unauthenticated remote attacker can cause the broker JVM to load and instantiate arbitrary classes available on its classpath with attacker-chosen String constructor arguments, before any broker-level authentication or authorization. With a suitable side-effecting class present (standard distributions bundle Spring and other libraries), this class-instantiation primitive can lead to remote code execution; even without a full RCE gadget it yields arbitrary side effects from constructors/static initializers and can be abused for denial of service. The same primitive is reachable from multiple command types and all supported protocol versions, so version negotiation or switching command types does not mitigate it.

candidate_title: Server-Side Request Forgery in the Link Checker transformation (unvalidated server-side GET to attacker-supplied URLs)
candidate_root_cause: The linkchecker transformation takes every external link found in rendered content and, instead of validating the target, enqueues it unchanged (LinkCheckerTransformation.transform, only checking reference.getType() == ResourceType.URL). A background thread dequeues items and hands the raw link reference to DefaultHTTPChecker.check(), which does new HttpGet(url) and httpClient.execute(httpGet) with no host/scheme/address validation. The only configured exclusion (rendering.transformation.linkchecker.excludedReferencePatterns) is matched exclusively against the source content reference (DefaultLinkCheckerThread.isExcluded is called with queueItem.getContentReference()), and the configuration interface documents the patterns as document references only, so there is no supported way to prevent requests to internal hosts; the check is not tied to the requesting user, is unauthenticated (cookies explicitly ignored, user agent "XWikiLinkChecker"), and is performed for any URL exposed in any rendered document.
candidate_impact: Blind (for plain viewers) server-side request forgery: the XWiki server can be made to issue requests to loopback, link-local, private, or otherwise internal HTTP(S) endpoints on behalf of an unprivileged content author, enabling internal port scanning and interaction with internal/unauthenticated HTTP services (including state-changing GET endpoints, cloud metadata endpoints reachable from the server, etc.). Because the HTTP response code is recorded in the LinkStateManager and exposed through the script API, actors able to evaluate scripts also get an SSRF oracle (reachability/status of internal hosts). Requests are sent without the attacker's credentials and with cookies ignored, so impact is that of an unauthenticated internal HTTP client rather than response-body exfiltration.

candidate_title: Link references with an unvalidated URI scheme (e.g. javascript:) are parsed and written verbatim into the rendered href attribute (XSS)
candidate_root_cause: The resource-reference layer types any string containing a 'scheme://' prefix as a URL without validating the scheme (URLResourceReferenceTypeParser.URL_SCHEME_PATTERN = "[a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*://"), and the XHTML link renderers then place the reference verbatim into the anchor's href attribute. XML-escaping is applied by the printer (so quotes cannot break out of the attribute), but the URI scheme is never restricted, so a scheme such as 'javascript:' is preserved into the produced markup. A second path reaches the same sink through interwiki references: when the interwiki alias is not present in the RenderingConfiguration definitions, InterWikiXHTMLLinkTypeRenderer falls back to writing the raw reference as the href. The XHTML parser has the same trust assumption: XWikiReferenceTagHandler.computeResourceReference maps an arbitrary href to ResourceType.URL (if it contains '://') or ResourceType.PATH otherwise, and the PATH/URL link type renderers write it back unchanged.
candidate_impact: Stored/DOM XSS in pages produced by the renderer: a user able to author content (without needing script or programming rights) can cause other users, including administrators, to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the wiki's origin when they activate the crafted link, enabling session/CSRF-token theft, actions with the victim's rights, and full compromise of the viewing account. The same unvalidated-scheme behaviour can be used for other dangerous URI schemes the embedding application does not expect (e.g. data: in additional contexts), and can defeat application-level expectations that the rendering layer emits only safe URL types.

candidate_title: Forced double OGNL evaluation of already-resolved UI tag attributes (`id`/`name`) in UIBean
candidate_root_cause: UIBean prematurely resolves tag attributes and later re-treats the resolved strings as OGNL expressions. (1) `UIBean.setId` evaluates the `id` attribute (`findString(id)`) and stores the resolved value in the component field `id`; `populateComponentHtmlId` later evaluates that same field again via `findStringIfAltSyntax(id)`. (2) `UIBean.evaluateParams` resolves `this.name` into the local `name` (`name = findString(this.name)`), then evaluates it again in `populateComponentHtmlId` (`findString(name)`) and in the nameValue block (`completeExpressionIfAltSyntax(name)` -> `findValue(..., valueClazz)`, and `findValue(name)` when valueClazz is null). `Component.findValue(String, String.class)` interprets any string containing `%{...}` as an expression and executes it through `TextParseUtil.translateVariables` -> `OgnlValueStack.findValue`, so data that merely came out of the first evaluation is executed as an OGNL expression in the second.
candidate_impact: Server-side execution of attacker-supplied text as an OGNL expression against the Struts value stack/action context. This is expression injection that permits access to server-side objects reachable from the value stack and, where the OGNL sandbox can be bypassed (the known exploit technique for this defect class), remote code execution. The review did not execute anything, so RCE is asserted only as the advisory-documented consequence of this defect class, not as a runtime-confirmed result.

candidate_title: SQL injection via unescaped `types` parameter in `DatabaseMetaData.getTables`
candidate_root_cause: In `org.sqlite.jdbc3.JDBC3DatabaseMetaData#getTables`, the caller-supplied `types` array is mapped into the query text as `"'" + t.toUpperCase() + "'"` (lines 1732-1738) without escaping single quotes, unlike the `tblNamePattern` path which is passed through `escape()` (lines 1680-1683). A value containing a single quote terminates the intended string literal and lets the entry change the query, so attacker-influenced `types` input is concatenated into SQL that the driver prepares and executes against the connection's database. The sibling helper `CoreDatabaseMetaData.quote()` (lines 158-164) has the same defect and is used to embed caller-supplied `catalog`/`schema`/`table` strings in `getImportedKeys`/`getExportedKeys`/`getCrossReference` (e.g. lines 1404-1415, 1151-1168), indicating a systematic missing-escape pattern in metadata SQL construction.
candidate_impact: Arbitrary single-statement SQL injection through a JDBC metadata call: confidentiality breach (UNION/expression-based reads of tables and attached schemas available to the connection), metadata/result tampering, and denial of service via expensive injected SELECTs. Because the driver's `executeQuery` compiles only the first statement (`sqlite3_prepare`), stacked statements such as `; DROP ...` are not executed through this path, which limits but does not remove the impact.

candidate_title: Untrusted URL dereference and predictable temp-file caching in `jdbc:sqlite::resource:` connection handling
candidate_root_cause: `SQLiteConnection.open()` treats everything after the `:resource:` prefix as a resource name, first resolving it through the thread context class loader and, if that fails, passing it directly to `new URL(resourceName)` with no protocol/host allow-list (SQLiteConnection.java:232-245). `extractResource()` then materializes the referenced content: for non-`file:` protocols it builds the destination as `System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir") + String.format("sqlite-jdbc-tmp-%d.db", resourceAddr.hashCode())` (lines 306-308) — a deterministic, guessable path in a commonly world-writable directory, created with default (typically 0644/umask-derived) permissions and never deleted. If that path already exists, the code returns the pre-existing file whenever `resourceAddr.openConnection().getLastModified()` is not strictly greater than the existing file's mtime (lines 310-322); for resources that send no Last-Modified header (and for many `jar:`/classpath URLs) `getLastModified()` is 0/-1, so any pre-planted file wins. Downloaded content is written with `Files.copy(reader, dbFile.toPath(), REPLACE_EXISTING)` without any integrity verification (lines 334-339); the MD5 comparison that would have detected substitution exists only as commented-out code (lines 324-331). The returned path is then handed to the native layer and opened as the database (lines 247-251, 279-286).
candidate_impact: Integrity/confidentiality of the data layer, plus a network-access primitive: (a) SSRF/URL-fetch driven by the connection string — the JVM performs requests (or reads arbitrary `file:`/`jar:` URLs) chosen by whoever controls the URL, reaching internal hosts/ports from the server context; (b) the fetched byte stream is handed to SQLite as a database, so attacker-chosen content becomes the database the application reads/writes (silent data substitution, forged rows/schema, and writes into other processes' cached copies since the path is reusable and not deleted); (c) local-attacker substitution: a pre-planted file at the predictable `/tmp/sqlite-jdbc-tmp-<hash>.db` path is preferred by the timestamp logic, so the application opens the attacker's database instead of the intended resource; (d) the cached copy is never removed and is created with default permissions, exposing the referenced database content to other local users.

candidate_title: Unauthenticated name-server config update can set configStorePath and overwrite/plant arbitrary files
candidate_root_cause: DefaultRequestProcessor.updateConfig (lines 557-596) only rejects properties containing "kvConfigPath" or "configStorePathName". "configStorePathName" is not a field of NamesrvConfig (or of any other config object) - the real field/key is "configStorePath" (NamesrvConfig lines 32-34, setter lines 83-85). The request body is parsed with MixAll.string2Properties (java.util.Properties semantics), merged by Configuration.update (only pre-existing keys survive mergeIfExist, and configStorePath is registered from NamesrvConfig), and applied via MixAll.properties2Object, which invokes setConfigStorePath with the attacker's string. NamesrvController (lines 69-74) then persists configuration through setStorePathFromConfig(namesrvConfig, "configStorePath"), so Configuration.persist()/getStorePath() resolves the destination path from the attacker-overwritten field and MixAll.string2File(allConfigs, attackerPath) writes there (also creating parent dirs, a .tmp and a .bak, deleting the previous target and renaming the temp file into place). The name server registers no ACL/RPCHook (unlike the broker), so no credential check blocks the request.
candidate_impact: Arbitrary file creation/overwrite (and destruction of the previous file plus creation of .tmp/.bak siblings) with attacker-influenced content, under the privileges of the name-server process. This can corrupt name-server/broker configuration, plant content in files the service account or other processes later read/execute, and, where permissions allow (user shell profile, authorized_keys, cron/scheduling files), plausibly lead to code execution as that user. It also overwrites the file before rename, so an existing file's content is lost even if the subsequent rename fails. The same handler also makes name-server config readable without authentication (GET_NAMESRV_CONFIG), which eases targeting.

candidate_title: Unauthenticated NameServer config update allows arbitrary-path file write because the config-path guard checks a non-existent property name
candidate_root_cause: DefaultRequestProcessor.updateConfig rejects only properties named `kvConfigPath` and `configStorePathName` (DefaultRequestProcessor.java:584). No config object defines a `configStorePathName` property: NamesrvConfig defines `configStorePath` (NamesrvConfig.java:34, getter/setter 79-85), so that half of the guard is dead code. NamesrvController.java:73 had already registered `namesrvConfig.configStorePath` as the Configuration store path (`setStorePathFromConfig(this.namesrvConfig, "configStorePath")`), therefore a request that sets `configStorePath` changes the target of Configuration.persist().
candidate_impact: Unauthenticated arbitrary-path file write/overwrite on the host running the NameServer, executed with the name-server process's privileges and with partially attacker-controlled content. Practical effects: overwrite or corrupt any file writable by that user (including the configuration file used at startup), persist attacker-chosen name-server settings such as `rocketmqHome` (not guarded either) which selects the logback configuration file loaded at next startup (NamesrvStartup.java:119) and `configStorePath` itself (NamesrvStartup.java:94 sets it from the -c file), and cause persistent denial of service. Because Properties escapes can inject additional lines, the primitive may support broader content control on some deployment layouts, creating a plausible secondary path to code execution where the service writes to files that are later executed or parsed by other system components; that escalation is a hypothesis, not established here.

candidate_title: Read-only API credentials can perform destructive/write operations because role enforcement ignores class-level @RolesAllowed and ORs class+method roles
candidate_root_cause: In `FF4jAuthorizationFilter.filter()`, authorization is only evaluated when the *resource method* itself carries `@RolesAllowed` (`isRolesAllowed()` checks `info.getResourceMethod().getAnnotation(RolesAllowed.class)`); if the method has no method-level annotation the filter simply returns and the request is allowed, regardless of the class-level `@RolesAllowed`. Additionally, `getRoles()` unions the class-level and method-level role arrays and the decision is `allowed if the user holds ANY role in the union`, so a class-level `READ` satisfies a method-level `WRITE`. The store resources declare only class-level `@RolesAllowed(ROLE_READ)` while exposing destructive POST endpoints (`/clear`, `/createSchema`, cache clear) with no method-level `WRITE` annotation, and `GroupResource` declares class-level READ with method-level WRITE on enable/disable — in all these cases a READ-only principal is accepted.
candidate_impact: Privilege escalation from read-only API access to full write/admin-equivalent operations: deletion of all feature flags and all properties (configuration/integrity loss, which can silently re-enable or disable protected functionality), execution of schema DDL, cache flushes, and group-wide enable/disable of features. The read-only/write separation that ApiConfig and the `@RolesAllowed` annotations are meant to provide is ineffective.

candidate_title: HTTP-controlled class name instantiated via Class.forName/newInstance for properties and flipping strategies (unsafe reflection) in ff4j console and Web API
candidate_root_cause: Externally supplied strings are used directly as class names and constructor arguments with no validation against the expected ff4j implementation classes. PropertyFactory.createProperty(name, type, value) does Class.forName(pType).getConstructor(String.class, String.class).newInstance(pName, pValue) (ff4j-core PropertyFactory.java:158-165), so the attacker chooses the class and both string parameters. MappingUtil.instanceFlippingStrategy(uid, className, params) does Class.forName(className).newInstance() then init() (MappingUtil.java:180-190). In both cases the constructor executes before the result is cast to Property/FlippingStrategy, so constructor side effects and class initialization occur regardless of the later ClassCastException.
candidate_impact: Attacker-selected classes are loaded and public constructors are invoked with attacker-controlled string arguments. With the JDK always available, java.io.PrintWriter/Formatter (String fileName, String csn) let an unauthorized caller create or truncate arbitrary files writable by the server process (configuration/log/asset destruction, plantable empty files, DoS) and, more generally, exercise any side-effecting (String,String) or no-arg constructor present on the classpath - the standard gadget surface for RCE. candidate_root_cause: BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable takes the class name and the message text directly from the wire and executes `Class clazz = Class.forName(className, false, <loader>); Constructor constructor = clazz.getConstructor(new Class[] {String.class}); return (Throwable) constructor.newInstance(new Object[] {message});` without first verifying that the resolved class is a Throwable subclass or otherwise allowlisted. candidate_title: Unauthenticated remote configuration update: broker UPDATE_BROKER_CONFIG reaches Runtime.exec via filter-server command, with the same unprotected update-config handler in NameServer/Controller
candidate_root_cause: Broker `AdminBrokerProcessor.updateBrokerConfig` (dispatched unconditionally from the request switch on `RequestCode.UPDATE_BROKER_CONFIG`) parses an attacker-supplied `key=value` body with `MixAll.string2Properties` and passes the whole `Properties` object to `org.apache.rocketmq.remoting.Configuration.update`, which (a) merges the values and (b) calls `MixAll.properties2Object(properties, configObject)` on every registered config object, reflectively invoking matching setters. There is no authorization check and no key allow-list/validation on the broker side, and Broker ACL is disabled by default (`BrokerConfig.aclEnable = false`; `BrokerController.initialAcl` returns immediately unless enabled). Consequently security-critical live settings are remotely writable: `BrokerConfig.rocketmqHome` (line 30) and `BrokerConfig.filterServerNums` (line 115). `FilterServerManager.buildStartCommand()` builds `String.format("sh %s/bin/startfsrv.sh %s", rocketmqHome, config)`; `FilterServerUtil.splitShellString` splits it on single spaces and `Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmdArray)` runs it. Because the command line itself contains `sh -c` tokens only if the attacker supplies them, a crafted `rocketmqHome` value injects `sh -c` arguments and the shell executes the attacker's command string (the referenced startfsrv.sh file need not exist). The same unprotected update-config handler pattern exists in the NameServer (`DefaultRequestProcessor.updateConfig`, which has no ACL hook registered at all) and the Controller (`ControllerRequestProcessor.updateControllerConfig`); there, attacker-chosen `kvConfigPath`/`configStorePath` combined with the unauthenticated `PUT_KV_CONFIG` request drives `KVConfigManager.persist()`/`Configuration.persist()` to write attacker-influenced content to attacker-chosen paths.
candidate_impact: Remote code execution with the privileges of the broker process (the filter-server shell is spawned by the broker JVM), i.e. full host compromise in deployments exposing the broker port without ACL (the default configuration). Secondary impact of the same root cause: attacker-directed file write/overwrite on NameServer and Controller via `kvConfigPath`/`configStorePath`; and remote tampering with any live broker/message-store configuration value (store paths, flow control, permissions), enabling data destruction or denial of service. The fact that `UPDATE_BROKER_CONFIG` is deliberately classified as an admin-only request code (`acl/common/Permission.ADMIN_CODE`) shows the operation is intended to be privileged, but the enforcement is absent in the default configuration.

candidate_root_cause: The broker registers AdminBrokerProcessor as the default processor (BrokerController.registerProcessor, lines 1079-1084) and AdminBrokerProcessor.updateBrokerConfig (765-801) parses the request body into java.util.Properties and passes it straight to Configuration.update (remoting/Configuration.java:179-203). Security-sensitive setters such as setRocketmqHome and setFilterServerNums are therefore reachable remotely. FilterServerManager.start (55-67) schedules createFilterServer every 30 s; once filterServerNums > 0 it builds `sh <rocketmqHome>/bin/startfsrv.sh ...` (buildStartCommand, 78-97) and FilterServerUtil.callShell (24-41) executes it via Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmdArray), so the attacker-controlled rocketmqHome string ends up inside a command run by the shell. The NameServer path is the same pattern with no ACL layer at all: DefaultRequestProcessor.updateConfig (603-636) applies arbitrary existing NamesrvConfig properties (e.g. rocketmqHome, kvConfigPath, configStorePath), and KVConfigManager.persist (90-112) then writes attacker-controlled JSON to the current kvConfigPath; NamesrvController registers this processor as the default processor (NamesrvController.java:216-226).
candidate_impact: On a default (ACL-disabled) broker, an unauthenticated network attacker can modify any existing broker/remoting/store configuration at runtime, and by setting filterServerNums>0 plus a crafted rocketmqHome can cause the broker to execute shell commands with the broker process privileges (typically root in common deployments). On the nameserver, the same unauthenticated update can alter nameserver configuration and redirect its KV-config persistence to an arbitrary filesystem path, yielding attacker-influenced file writes and persistent configuration tampering. Even where the shell chain is not used, arbitrary live-config tampering of a core messaging component is a high-impact integrity/availability issue.

candidate_root_cause: ControllerPreAuthenticatedGatewaySecurityTokenFilter builds the pre-auth credentials as HeaderAuthentication(controllerId, <tenant-configured gateway token>) without checking that the configured token is non-empty (hawkbit-security-integration/.../ControllerPreAuthenticatedGatewaySecurityTokenFilter.java:72-77). candidate_title: Missing XXE/DTD hardening in XML parsing entry points: XLS spreadsheet parsers (XLSXmlParser, XLSXmlNormaliser) use a default DocumentBuilderFactory, and the DSTU2 format parser still processes DTD declarations unlike its five hardened sibling modules
candidate_root_cause: One root cause: XML parser instances are created with DTD processing / external-entity resolution left enabled, i.e. the project's own XXE hardening was not applied everywhere. (a) XLSXmlParser.parseXml and XLSXmlNormaliser.parseXml call DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance(), set only setNamespaceAware(true) and pass the caller's InputStream straight to builder.parse(), so JDK/Xerces defaults (DOCTYPE allowed, external general/parameter entities and external DTD loading on) apply. (b) org.hl7.fhir.dstu2.formats.XmlParserBase.loadXml omits factory.setFeature(XmlPullParser.FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL, false) and its nextNoWhitespace silently skips XmlPullParser.DOCDECL events, whereas all five sibling modules (dstu2016may, dstu3, r4, r4b, r5) set FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL=false (e.g. dstu2016may line 210) and throw 'DTD declarations are not allowed' on DOCDECL (dstu2016may lines 235-237; same code in dstu3/r4/r4b/r5).
candidate_impact: Improper restriction of XML external entities: parsing attacker-supplied XML can disclose local files (content substituted into parsed cell/text values, and re-serialized by XLSXmlNormaliser), cause server-side requests/outbound connections via external entity/DTD references, and enable entity-expansion denial of service. For DSTU2 the exposure applies to any process that parses DSTU2 XML (validator/convertor CLI and downstream HAPI DSTU2 servers); for the XLS classes it applies to downstream tooling that consumes the published utilities API.

candidate_root_cause: GenericFilter is activated for every provider-side service and intercepts any $invoke call on a non-GenericService (GenericFilter.java:54-57). candidate_impact: Remote code execution in the provider JVM under the provider's privileges: arbitrary class instantiation plus attacker-chosen public setter/field writes (JNDI injection via com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl.setDataSourceName/setAutoCommit and similar bean gadgets, or a JDK-deserialization gadget chain through the nativejava path). candidate_title: Provider-side generic invocation ($invoke) trusts attacker-controlled classes and performs arbitrary instantiation/property writes (potential RCE)
candidate_root_cause: The provider-side GenericFilter processes any $invoke request on a non-GenericService interface and converts the caller-supplied argument array according to caller-selected semantics. In the default generic mode it calls PojoUtils.realize, whose realize0() takes a 'class' key from an attacker-supplied Map and overwrites the declared parameter type with ClassHelper.forName(<attacker string>) (PojoUtils.java:371-379); the converted value is then instantiated when it is not assignable to the map (PojoUtils.java:390-402) and instantiated again at PojoUtils.java:437, after which every map entry is matched to a public setter and invoked with the attacker value (PojoUtils.java:439-458) or written directly into the (possibly private) target field (PojoUtils.java:459-465). The 'bean' branch calls JavaBeanSerializeUtil.deserialize, which resolves beanDescriptor.getClassName() and instantiates it (JavaBeanSerializeUtil.java:369-410) and then invokes setters/writes fields from the descriptor (JavaBeanSerializeUtil.java:253-290, 296-313). The 'nativejava' branch performs raw JDK readObject() on attacker bytes (GenericFilter.java:81-83). No allowlist or assignability check exists that restricts these operations to the service's declared parameter types; the only class filter (SerialDetector) is not used by PojoUtils/JavaBeanSerializeUtil and is report-only by default (SerialDetector.java:100-113).
candidate_impact: Remote code execution in the provider process is achievable through standard gadget patterns: a class instantiated by PojoUtils/JavaBeanSerializeUtil whose property setter performs a JNDI/LDAP/RMI lookup, or a Java serialization gadget chain delivered through the nativejava branch, can execute attacker code in the provider JVM. Even without a working gadget, the provider is coerced into arbitrary class loading, instantiation (including private constructors in PojoUtils.newInstance and JavaBeanSerializeUtil.instantiate) and arbitrary setter/private-field writes on its classpath, which is a powerful primitive and may corrupt provider state. The nativejava branch also lets a consumer bypass the transport-level serialization-id restriction (the transport is normally hessian2) by embedding a Java-serialized blob inside an argument.
cwe_name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

candidate_title: S3 TransferManager.downloadDirectory containment check bypass (path traversal) in aws-java-sdk-s3
candidate_root_cause: TransferManager.downloadDirectory() iterates S3 object summaries and writes each object to `new File(destinationDirectory, summary.getKey())` (line 1472) after validating the key with leavesRoot(). leavesRoot() returns `!new File(localBaseDirectory, key).getCanonicalPath().startsWith(localBaseDirectory.getCanonicalPath())` (line 1515). Because the comparison is a raw String prefix check with no path-separator boundary (e.g., no `+ File.separator` and no java.nio.file.Path.startsWith), any object key whose canonicalized path begins with the same characters as the destination directory is accepted even when it is outside that directory. Example: destination `/home/u/downloads` plus key `../downloads-evil/payload` canonicalizes to `/home/u/downloads-evil/payload`, which `startsWith("/home/u/downloads")` matches, so the guard returns false and the download proceeds to that outside path. If the destination canonical path is "/" (or a very short prefix), the guard is effectively vacuous. The check is the only containment control in this code path; there is no second validation in prepareDownload/DownloadCallable/S3CryptoModule paths (repo-wide search for getCanonicalPath() finds only this one occurrence in main code).
candidate_impact: Arbitrary file write outside the intended download directory (constrained to paths whose canonical form string-prefix-matches the destination, or unbounded when the destination canonical path is a short/root prefix). Consequences include overwriting files the application did not intend to touch (data corruption/destruction, integrity violation, potentially planting files in other directories if those paths share the prefix and are writable), which in some deployments can escalate to code execution or configuration tampering. This is an attacker-controlled remote-input-to-local-file sink in a widely used download API.
cwe_name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

candidate_json: {"title": "S3 TransferManager.downloadDirectory containment check bypass (path traversal) in aws-java-sdk-s3", "cwe": null, "root_cause": "TransferManager.downloadDirectory() iterates S3 object summaries and writes each object to `new File(destinationDirectory, summary.getKey())` (line 1472) after validating the key with leavesRoot(). leavesRoot() returns `!new File(localBaseDirectory, key).getCanonicalPath().startsWith(localBaseDirectory.getCanonicalPath())` (line 1515). Because the comparison is a raw String prefix check with no path-separator boundary (e.g., no `+ File.separator` and no java.nio.file.Path.startsWith), any object key whose canonicalized path begins with the same characters as the destination directory is accepted even when it is outside that directory. Example: destination `/home/u/downloads` plus key `../downloads-evil/payload` canonicalizes to `/home/u/downloads-evil/payload`, which `startsWith(\"/home/u/downloads\")` matches, so the guard returns false and the download proceeds to that outside path. If the destination canonical path is \"/\" (or a very short prefix), the guard is effectively vacuous. The check is the only containment control in this code path; there is no second validation in prepareDownload/DownloadCallable/S3CryptoModule paths (repo-wide search for getCanonicalPath() finds only this one occurrence in main code).", "impact": "Arbitrary file write outside the intended download directory (constrained to paths whose canonical form string-prefix-matches the destination, or unbounded when the destination canonical path is a short/root prefix). Consequences include overwriting files the application did not intend to touch (data corruption/destruction, integrity violation, potentially planting files in other directories if those paths share the prefix and are writable), which in some deployments can escalate to code execution or configuration tampering. This is an attacker-controlled remote-input-to-local-file sink in a widely used download API.", "affected_locations": null}

candidate_title: Unvalidated ARN `region` interpolated into S3 access-point endpoint host allows request redirection (SSRF/host injection)
candidate_root_cause: S3 ARN support parses `region` from the caller-supplied bucket ARN without any hostname/format validation and later interpolates it directly into the request hostname, while all sibling hostname components (accountId, accessPointName, outpostId) are validated with HostnameValidator.validateHostnameCompliant. In AmazonS3Client.validateS3ResourceArn the equality check between the ARN region and the client region is skipped when useArnRegion() is true or forceGlobalBucketAccess is enabled, so an attacker-shaped ARN region reaches the endpoint builders.
candidate_impact: Server-side request forgery / request redirection: an application that passes an attacker-influenced bucket ARN to the SDK can cause the SDK to connect (TLS server-auth against the attacker's own validly-certified domain) and send a request signed with the application's AWS credentials, exposing the SigV4 Authorization material (access key ID, signature, signed headers), the temporary session token header when applicable, the object key/path and any caller data, and letting the attacker return attacker-controlled responses to the SDK. A malformed non-resolvable region instead yields an unhandled exception/invalid-endpoint failure (availability/robustness side effect).

The JAXB/JAX-RS unmarshaller and the Aegis XOP type pass the raw `href` attribute from the request XML directly into these helpers, so a remote caller chooses the URL that the server resolves and reads.

candidate_title: SSRF: HTTP-poll input (JSON path input) fetches attacker-controlled URLs without URL-whitelist enforcement
candidate_root_cause: HttpPollTransport builds and executes an OkHttp GET directly from the input configuration value `target_url` (and attacker-supplied `headers`) and never consults UrlWhitelistService. It is the only user-configurable outbound HTTP fetcher in the repo that does not enforce the URL whitelist that Graylog applies elsewhere (HTTPJSONPathDataAdapter.doGet lines 160-166, DSVHTTPDataAdapter lines 99-104/116, HTTPEventNotification.execute lines 107-112, HTTPAlarmCallback lines 90-92). The whitelist dependency is simply absent from HttpPollTransport's constructor (lines 88-101), so there is no check at configuration time or at request time. The fetched body is decoded by JsonPathCodec and stored as log messages, turning a blind SSRF into an exfiltration-capable one.
candidate_impact: Server-side requests from the Graylog host to arbitrary destinations that are otherwise unreachable by the attacker: loopback/internal admin APIs, RFC1918 services, and cloud instance-metadata endpoints that return JSON (e.g. credential endpoints). Because the response is decoded into messages the attacker can read, the attacker can exfiltrate internal response data; arbitrary request headers also permit authenticated/credentialed requests to internal services. This defeats the network segmentation between the Graylog server and internal networks. Secondary effect: internal GET endpoints reachable only from the server can be triggered/abused (SSRF chaining), and HTTP redirects are followed by default (OkHttp default; OkHttpClientProvider lines 88-93 never disables them), so even a benign target that issues redirects can be used to pivot.

candidate_title: SSRF: unauthenticated instance registration lets a rogue registrant choose arbitrary absolute URLs that the server fetches and proxies back
candidate_root_cause: The server trusts any URL supplied in a Registration. `InstancesController.register` (lines 76-85) accepts an arbitrary registration and only overwrites `source` (no authentication/authorization/allow-list in the module; `spring-boot-starter-security` is test-scope only in the server poms). `Registration.checkUrl` (lines 91-99) merely requires `new URI(url).isAbsolute()`, so any scheme/host/path (cloud metadata IPs, internal hostnames, loopback, etc.) is accepted. `Instance` (lines 105-106) always installs the registration `healthUrl` as the `health` endpoint, and `InstanceExchangeFilterFunctions.rewriteEndpointUrl`/`rewriteUrl` (lines 75-112) uses the stored endpoint URL as the base for proxied requests, so the URL and host are fully registrant-controlled. `InstanceWebProxy.forward` (lines 91-122) then performs the request with the server's network position and the proxy controllers stream the fetched body back to the caller. `QueryIndexEndpointStrategy.convertResponse` (lines 113-118) additionally stores any absolute `_links[].href` returned by the registrant as new endpoints, removing the need to know a matching endpoint URL.
candidate_impact: The SBA server becomes a proxy into its own network: internal services and non-public admin interfaces can be reached and their responses read, cloud instance-metadata endpoints can be queried (credential theft), and internal hosts/ports can be enumerated via response timing/status. Background updaters amplify the requests without any further attacker action. A rogue registration can also cause the server to send configured instance credentials (BasicAuthHttpHeaderProvider) to the attacker URL.

candidate_title: Client-supplied registration identity and URLs are trusted for outbound requests and instance-credential selection (SSRF + Basic-credential disclosure)
candidate_root_cause: The server derives the outbound destination and the credential identity from data that the registering client fully controls, without any authorization or binding between the two. Registration (name/healthUrl/managementUrl/metadata) is accepted by POST /instances with only a syntactic check (Registration.checkUrl requires merely uri.isAbsolute()), the registration is keyed only by SHA-1 of the client-supplied healthUrl (HashingInstanceUrlIdGenerator), and StatusUpdater/InfoUpdater/QueryIndexEndpointStrategy then issue HTTP requests to those client-supplied URLs. In addition, BasicAuthHttpHeaderProvider.getHeaders selects credentials with serviceMap.get(instance.getRegistration().getName()) or the configured default credentials, i.e. the client-claimed service name, and the addHeaders filter attaches the resulting Authorization header to every request made for that instance. Actuator-index hrefs are adopted verbatim (QueryIndexEndpointStrategy.convertResponse; alignWithManagementUrl only rewrites http->https, never checks origin), and InstanceExchangeFilterFunctions.rewriteEndpointUrl/rewriteUrl plus InstanceWebProxy then forward caller-controlled method/path/query/body/headers to those URLs.
candidate_impact: Disclosure of the admin server's configured per-service/default Basic-auth credentials to an attacker-chosen origin (those credentials normally unlock the protected actuator endpoints of the impersonated monitored services, so the attacker can pivot to those services). Additionally, the admin server can be used as an SSRF pivot from its own network position: its monitoring loop performs GET/OPTIONS requests to attacker-specified hosts, and the proxy path allows arbitrary methods, paths, queries and request bodies to attacker-supplied absolute URLs, enabling internal port scanning and access to services reachable only from the admin server (including cloud metadata endpoints).

candidate_title: EJB Invoker legacy servlet does not enforce its role check, allowing unauthorized EJB method invocation

candidate_root_cause: The pod file-transfer implementation builds shell command strings by direct concatenation/String.format of context-supplied path values and runs them via exec("sh", "-c", ...) with no quoting or escaping. candidate_title: Unsafe SnakeYAML deserialization in Serialization.unmarshalYaml (default Constructor allows arbitrary type instantiation)
candidate_root_cause: Serialization.unmarshalYaml constructs SnakeYAML with the default `new Yaml()` (no SafeConstructor / no allowed-type restriction) and feeds it the raw input stream (`yaml.load(is)`) before converting to JSON. candidate_title: SWITCH task condition is evaluated as unsandboxed JavaScript in the master JVM (code execution via Nashorn Java interop)
candidate_root_cause: `SwitchTaskUtils` creates a generic JSR-223 engine via `new ScriptEngineManager().getEngineByName("js")` and calls `engine.eval(expression)` (line 35) with no sandbox, class filter, or SecurityManager. The expression is the SWITCH task's `condition` string from the task definition: `SwitchLogicTask.calculateConditionResult()` evaluates each `SwitchResultVo.getCondition()` after replacing single quotes with double quotes and substituting `${param}` placeholders (`setTaskParams`). Nothing constrains the condition to an expression-only grammar: `SwitchParameters` is deserialized from the user-supplied `taskParams` JSON, `checkParameters()` unconditionally returns true, and `TaskDefinitionServiceImpl.checkTaskDefinitionValid()` only checks project ACLs, not task parameter content. On Java 8 (Nashorn) the evaluated script can access `Java.type(...)`, `Packages...`, etc., so the condition can construct and invoke arbitrary Java classes in the master process.
candidate_impact: Arbitrary code execution as the OS user running the master server, from a workflow-author-level account. The master JVM handles workflow scheduling and holds DB/registry credentials, so this enables full compromise of the scheduling cluster (credential theft, workflow/data tampering, lateral movement), bypassing the intended model where user task code executes on workers under a tenant identity.

candidate_title: redirect_uri is validated in decoded/normalized form but the original encoded form is returned, allowing open redirect and authorization-response leakage (wildcard clients)
candidate_root_cause: In RedirectUtils.verifyRedirectUri (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/utils/RedirectUtils.java:92-154) the value is validated only after decodeRedirectUri() decodes percent-encodings up to 5 times and getNormalizedRedirectUri() normalizes/lowercases it (lines 109-117, using matchesRedirects with allowWildcards=true). Afterwards the method normalizes and returns the ORIGINAL, still-encoded redirectUri (lines 135-146) without ever verifying that the original and the decoded form have the same scheme/host/port (there is no userinfo/origin check anywhere in the flow). The fallback exact comparison at lines 139-141 runs only when the decoded form did not already match (and with wildcards disabled), so a wildcard match on the decoded form is sufficient to make the original encoded value pass. Because matchesRedirects (lines 232-248) treats a configured value ending in '*' as a raw string prefix, an encoded form such as '<valid-host>%2f@<attacker-host>/...' decodes to '<valid-host>/@<attacker-host>/...' (which matches the '<valid-host>/' wildcard prefix) while the unvalidated original is the string handed to the browser, which parses the last '@' in the authority as the userinfo separator and therefore navigates to <attacker-host>.
candidate_impact: Unauthenticated open redirect from the identity provider's own trusted login endpoint; in standard flow the victim's browser is sent to an attacker-controlled origin with the authorization `code` (and `session_state`/`state`) as query parameters, and in implicit/hybrid flows access/ID tokens are placed in the fragment where attacker JavaScript can read them. This enables authorization-code/token theft where PKCE or client secrets do not protect the redirect leg, plus convincing phishing that originates from the legitimate Keycloak URL. Redirect validation is also reused for post_logout_redirect_uri (LogoutEndpoint), request_uri allow-lists (PAR/CIBA/request-object), action tokens, and the account/identity-broker referrer flows, so the same mismatch affects those callers.
cwe_name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

candidate_title: Gzip resource-cache path confinement uses a bare string prefix, letting attacker-influenced theme resource paths escape the cache directory
candidate_root_cause: GzipResourceEncodingProvider.getEncodedStream builds a cache file path by concatenating cacheDir + the caller-supplied path segments and then authorizes it with encodedFile.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(cacheDir.getCanonicalPath()) (line 41). No separator/Path boundary is required, so a canonical path that merely shares the cache directory string as a prefix (e.g. a sibling directory such as '<tmp>/kc-gzip-cacheX/...' reached through '..') passes confinement. The same check in FolderTheme (services/.../theme/FolderTheme.java line 96) and FolderThemeProvider (line 89) appends File.separator, showing the intended stricter form; this call site omits it. The resulting File is then opened for reading at line 78, and, when the producer returns data, is used as a write target at lines 45-76 (parent.mkdirs() + move).
candidate_impact: Path traversal outside the intended per-version gzip cache directory, limited to directories whose absolute path shares the cache-dir string prefix. Read disclosure of '.gz' files in such locations (confidentiality), and in the producer-write branch possible creation/replacement of a '.gz' file at a path in such a location (integrity). Ordinary traversal to arbitrary files (e.g. ../../etc/passwd) is still blocked by the canonical check, so this should not be described as unrestricted arbitrary-file read.

candidate_title: Path traversal / arbitrary file read via JobManager custom log REST handler
candidate_root_cause: JobManagerCustomLogHandler.getFile() builds the file to serve as `new File(logDir, filename)` directly from the `:filename` path parameter, and LogFileNamePathParameter.convertFromString() performs no validation (returns the raw token). Because RouterHandler passes the already-decoded request path into Router, and Router.decodePathTokens() splits that path on '/' and then URL-decodes every token a second time, a double-encoded separator (`%252F`) survives the first decode as `%2F`, does not split the token, and is decoded to a real '/' inside the `filename` value when the route `/jobmanager/logs/:filename` is matched. The resulting value can therefore contain `../` sequences that escape the configured log directory. AbstractJobManagerFileHandler then serves any `file != null && file.exists()` without a canonical-path containment check, and HandlerUtils.transferFile streams the file contents back to the HTTP client.
candidate_impact: Unauthenticated information disclosure: any file readable by the JobManager process can be downloaded, e.g. `flink-conf.yaml` (Kerberos/ZooKeeper/BlobStore/RocksDB credentials, state backend paths), TLS keystores/truststores, the JobManager log itself, or system files such as `/etc/passwd`. This crosses the intended boundary of serving only files from the configured log directory and is a high-impact confidentiality issue for an exposed cluster.
cwe_name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

candidate_root_cause: Camel creates XML parser factories for attacker-controlled message bodies without fully disabling DTD/external-entity resolution. In camel-core, XmlConverter.createDocumentBuilderFactory() and createSAXParserFactory() disable only "external-general-entities" while leaving external-parameter-entities and DOCTYPE processing enabled, so parameter-entity based XXE/DTD attacks remain possible on the default DOM/SAX conversion paths.

Availability: entity-expansion/DTD denial of service. StAX parsing happens before any application validation, and successful entity expansion can also feed attacker-chosen content into downstream JAXB unmarshalling.

In camel-netty-http and camel-netty4-http the deserialization is gated by `transferException` alone: NettyHttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream uses a plain `new ObjectInputStream(is).readObject()` with no allow-list and no allow option, and in the producer path the object is deserialized *before* the `instanceof Exception` check, so any gadget class is instantiated.
candidate_impact: Remote code execution in the Camel application JVM via Java deserialization gadget chains; also arbitrary object injection into exchanges/exception propagation, and denial of service. Producer-side exploitation allows a malicious or compromised HTTP server (or MITM) to execute code on the Camel client; consumer-side allows any network client to do so when the flag is enabled.

candidate_title: Untrusted JNDI Initial Context configuration in JndiJmsConnectionFactoryHandler enables JNDI injection / potential RCE
candidate_root_cause: JndiJmsConnectionFactoryHandler.createInitialContext() copies configuration-supplied values for `java.naming.factory.initial` (JNDI_INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY) and `java.naming.provider.url` (JNDI_PROVIDER_URL), plus every dynamic property, into the JNDI environment Hashtable with no allowlist of context-factory classes or provider-URL schemes, then constructs `new InitialContext(env)` (line 133) and calls `initialContext.lookup(factoryName)` (line 91). Both properties are required, non-empty, and support Expression Language over the variable registry (JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProperties lines 34-50), and JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProvider wires the handler in on enable (lines 56-59). candidate_title: Ineffective JNDI provider URL scheme allow-list in JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProvider (substring comparison, plus accept-by-default for non-URL inputs) enables unsafe remote JNDI resolution/deserialization
candidate_root_cause: JndiJmsProviderUrlValidator.isSchemeAllowed() iterates the allowed set and tests `allowedScheme.contains(scheme)` instead of `allowedSchemes.contains(scheme)` (equality), so any scheme that is a substring of an allowed scheme (e.g. "t", "s", "t3", "sl", "ud", "file", "jgroups", "vm") passes validation. In addition, isUrlAllowed() returns `allowed = true` whenever the regex `^([^:]+)://.+$` does not match, so provider URLs that omit the "//" form (and other non-matching spellings) are never scheme-checked. The documented contract (additionalDetails.html lines 104-119) and the property description state that only the exact schemes file/jgroups/ssl/t3/t3s/tcp/udp/vm are allowed, and the Java system property override is documented as a space-separated list of schemes, so the code contradicts its own specification.
candidate_impact: Defeat of the JNDI provider-URL restriction intended to prevent untrusted remote JNDI resolution. Where a reachable remote provider (e.g. LDAP/RMI-style naming service, or another scheme accepted by the configured initial context factory) can be reached, the NiFi host may deserialize objects returned by that service, which is a well-known path to remote code execution under the NiFi process account; at minimum it enables SSRF to arbitrary naming-service endpoints, credential exposure (JNDI environment including principal/credentials is sent to the attacker-chosen provider), and disclosure of class/type information.

candidate_title: ExtractCCDAAttributes parses untrusted FlowFile XML without XXE protections (external entities/DTD resolution enabled)

candidate_impact: Where the dependency parser resolves external entities, a crafted CDA document can cause the NiFi process to read local files reachable by the NiFi OS user (for example configuration files that contain keystore/truststore locations and other sensitive properties) or to issue server-side requests to internal HTTP/HTTPS/file endpoints (SSRF), with the retrieved text potentially surfaced through the generated FlowFile attributes. candidate_impact: Remote code execution in the NiFi JVM as the NiFi operating-system account (typically a service account with access to flow data, repositories, keystores/truststores, cluster credentials and the configuration database); it is a privilege escalation past the intended authorization boundary because NiFi distinguishes code-executing components via the @Restricted annotation, which these services lack. Only integrity/availability of the host and confidentiality of all NiFi-managed data and secrets need be assumed.

candidate_title: Missing authorization on resource-center file read/edit/download endpoints allows any authenticated user to read and overwrite other users' resource files
candidate_root_cause: Resource file operations are addressed by a global resourceId with no permission check. ResourcesServiceImpl.readResource(int resourceId, ...), updateResourceContent(int resourceId, String content) and downloadResource(int resourceId) do not accept the login user and never compare the resource owner (resource.getUserId()) with the caller, even though Resource rows carry an owning user, ResourceMapper pagination is filtered by owner/authorization, and sibling operations (updateResource at ResourcesServiceImpl.java:321-324, delete at :733-736, verifyPid at :1034-1037) call hasPerm(loginUser, resource.getUserId()). The controllers likewise forward only the path id and drop the already-available loginUser (ResourcesController.java:366-371, :424-432, :450-452). Because Resource objects are returned to the caller, an attacker can enumerate ids to reach any user's/tenant's files.
candidate_impact: Cross-user/cross-tenant confidentiality and integrity breach of the resource center: reading other users' scripts/configs and downloading their files, and silently overwriting the content of arbitrary resources. candidate_title: Unescaped relation identifier interpolated into superuser SQL in AlterTableOperation.getRowCount
candidate_root_cause: AlterTableOperation.getRowCount composes SQL by string interpolation: String.format(Locale.ENGLISH, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM \"%s\".\"%s\"", ident.schema(), ident.name()) and executes it via Sessions.newSystemSession(), whose session user is User.CRATE_USER (superuser). candidate_title: Missing authorization on REST Process deletion (/api/system/processes/{id})
candidate_root_cause: ProcessRestRepository.delete(Context, Integer) overrides the protected DSpaceRestRepository.delete method with no @PreAuthorize annotation, unlike most other write endpoints in the same class and in sibling repositories. The HTTP path RestResourceController.delete → deleteInternal → DSpaceRestRepository.deleteById → getThisRepository().delete(context, id) therefore reaches it with no method-security check. ProcessServiceImpl.delete performs authorization only implicitly, via BitstreamService.delete → authorizeService.authorizeAction on each attached bitstream; it never authorizes deletion of the Process row/entity. For a process with no attached bitstreams (e.g., a queued/running job or any script run that produced no file), processDAO.delete(context, process) runs for any caller. ProcessRestPermissionEvaluatorPlugin implements owner-or-admin semantics for the 'PROCESS' type but no code path requests a DELETE permission for it, leaving the delete endpoint unprotected.
candidate_impact: Unauthorized destruction of script-process records (and of their tracking/history) for any process having no bitstreams; this includes queued/running jobs and file-less scripts, so it can corrupt or abort in-flight administrative/background work (availability/integrity impact, potential workflow-state inconsistencies when the still-running script later updates its deleted Process row). It does not grant code execution or disclosure. Processes with attached bitstreams are partly shielded by the per-bitstream DELETE policy check.

candidate_title: Missing METADATA_READ authorization in REST search method BitstreamRestRepository.findByItemHandle (bitstream metadata disclosure)
candidate_root_cause: BitstreamRestRepository.findByItemHandle (dspace-server-webapp, exposed as /api/core/bitstreams/search/byItemHandle) resolves an Item from a caller-supplied handle and then collects all Bitstreams of all Bundles via item.getBundles()/bundle.getBitstreams() and returns converter.toRest(matchedBitstream,...) without any authorization check. The method has no @PreAuthorize and performs no in-body permission check, even though its javadoc explicitly promises the check ('will be returned if the user has "METADATA_READ" access') and the class declares an @Autowired AuthorizeService field that is unused anywhere in the file - the exact leftover expected if the documented check was removed. Compare findOne (line 92: hasPermission(#id,'BITSTREAM','METADATA_READ')) and the BitstreamFormat/accessStatus link repositories, which all enforce METADATA_READ, and BitstreamMetadataReadPermissionEvaluatorPlugin which defines exactly the semantics (admin, or READ on bitstream, or READ on parent item AND first bundle).
candidate_impact: Information disclosure of restricted-file metadata: file names, sizes, checksum values (MD5/SHA), bundle and format information, bitstream UUIDs, sequence numbers and the derived /content URL of bitstreams in items/bundles the requester is not allowed to read (e.g. restricted/embargoed resources, withdrawn items reachable via their public handle). Checksums and exact names can be used to confirm the identity of known files and to map a repository's hidden holdings; it also makes restricted items' file inventories enumerable without any account. Integrity of the stored content is not directly affected.

candidate_title: HTTP client conduits retain Authorization/Proxy-Authorization (and session cookies) when following a redirect to a different host
candidate_root_cause: CXF's HTTP client conduits follow 3xx redirects themselves, but the outgoing request state (the Headers object backed by Message.PROTOCOL_HEADERS, plus Cookiess session cookies) belongs to the conduit/message rather than to the redirect target. When a redirect is followed, the request is re-issued from that same state, so credentials configured for the original endpoint (AuthorizationPolicy / HttpAuthSupplier preemptive Basic-Digest-Negotiate, or an application/AccessToken header) are retained and sent to the Location target, including a different host. The only stripping primitive, Headers.removeAuthorizationHeaders(), exists but is never invoked in the visible source; the redirect-handling code that must call it lives in the filtered *Conduit.java classes.
candidate_impact: Disclosure of HTTP Basic/Digest/Negotiate credentials or bearer tokens to an attacker-selected host, enabling credential theft/session hijacking; with maintained sessions, cookies are replayed to the redirect target as well. Because the redirect target is fully attacker-controlled, this can also be pivoted toward internal hosts (SSRF-like requests carrying the victim's credentials).

candidate_title: Netty HTTP client validates TLS certificate chain but not the server hostname (CWE-295)
candidate_root_cause: For HTTPS calls made through the Netty transport, the client SSLEngine is built by SSLUtils.createClientSSLEngine(...), which calls SSLUtils.getSSLContext(parameters) (i.e. addHNV=false) and then SSLContext.createSSLEngine() with no peer host; the resulting engine is wrapped in `new SslHandler(sslEngine)` by NettyHttpClientPipelineFactory.configureClientSSLOnDemand(...) without setting `endpointIdentificationAlgorithm = "HTTPS"` (the only occurrences of EndpointIdentificationAlgorithm in the tree are the deliberate disable in SSLUtils and a Jetty server comment). Netty does not perform hostname verification itself, so a certificate issued by any trusted CA for a different hostname is accepted for the target host. The HTTP/2 branch builds the engine via SslContextBuilder.forClient()...newEngine(channel.alloc()) with the same omission.
candidate_impact: Man-in-the-middle/impersonation of HTTPS services contacted by CXF clients using the Netty transport: confidentiality and integrity of SOAP/REST traffic is lost whenever the attacker presents any certificate signed by a CA the client trusts for another name; credentials sent over the channel (Basic/Digest/OAuth tokens) can be captured or responses modified. Fails to meet the hostname-verification requirement of RFC 6125 / Java's default HttpsURLConnection behavior.

candidate_title: Untrusted repository parameters drive JNDI lookup in JndiRepositoryFactory (JNDI injection; mitigated by disabled-by-default JCR-5135 gate)
candidate_root_cause: `JndiRepositoryFactory.getRepository(Map)` converts caller-supplied repository settings directly into a JNDI environment and lookup: any `org.apache.jackrabbit.repository.jndi.name` value becomes the JNDI name, and for a `jndi:` repository URI the URI authority is copied verbatim into `Context.INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY` (line 115). `getRepository(name, environment)` then executes `new InitialContext(environment).lookup(name)` (line 124). Because both the context factory and the lookup name are attacker-influenceable, a crafted value (e.g. an LDAP/RMI URL) causes the JVM to resolve a remote context and load/execute remote classes (RemoteObject factory / codebase), i.e. RCE in the process that resolves the repository. The same sink exists in `org.apache.jackrabbit.commons.repository.JNDIRepositoryFactory.getRepository()` (line 67) and in `RegistryHelper.unregisterRepository()` (line 101, `ctx.lookup(name)`), all three of which are gated by the shared `JNDI_ENABLED` constant. The source documents this history: `JndiRepositoryFactory` line 60 says "Disabled by default, see JCR-5135".
candidate_impact: Remote code execution (or at least attacker-directed class loading / deserialization) in the process that resolves the JCR repository, as well as SSRF-style access to internal JNDI services, when JNDI lookups are enabled and the repository parameters come from an untrusted source. If treated as the historical JCR-5135 issue, this is the code location the project disabled by default to remove the RCE exposure.

candidate_title: Cross-user WebDAV/JCR session hijacking via public session-scoped lock tokens used as session-cache handles
candidate_root_cause: JCRWebdavServer.SessionCache.get() treats request-supplied lock tokens (Lock-Token header and If-header tokens) as bearer handles and returns the cached JCR repository session of whoever registered that token, without any credential check. DefaultItemCollection.lock() registers the DAV lock token of a session-scoped JCR lock as a session reference; for session-scoped locks LockImpl.getLockToken() returns null, so LockTokenMapper.getDavLocktoken() derives the token deterministically as 'opaquelocktoken:4403ef44-4124-11e1-b965-00059a3c7a00:<node identifier>'. That derived token is not a secret: it is embedded in the DAV:lockdiscovery property (AbstractActiveLock.toXml -> JcrActiveLock.getToken()) that is served to every session able to read the locked node, and it can also be recomputed from the node identifier. Combining a non-secret token with token-based session lookup lets any other user (or an unauthenticated client) obtain the lock owner's cached repository session.
candidate_impact: Authentication and authorization bypass: an unauthenticated or low-privileged attacker can operate with the victim's repository session for as long as the session-scoped lock keeps that session cached, i.e., read, modify, move, delete, lock/unlock and query content with the victim's privileges (including administrative sessions). This is cross-user session hijacking/privilege escalation on a network-facing component, and it also allows the attacker to consume/abuse the victim's session rather than just the lock.

candidate_title: Write-enabled DefaultServlet accepts partial PUT (Content-Range) to create/overwrite webapp files with attacker-controlled content
candidate_root_cause: DefaultServlet.doPut() delegates a request carrying a Content-Range header to executePartialPut(), which builds a temporary file whose length is set from the attacker-supplied range length, seeks to the attacker-supplied start offset, copies the request body into it, and then hands it to resources.write(path, stream, true) (overwrite=true). parseContentRange() only validates header syntax/ordering (ContentRange.isValid(): start >= 0, end >= start, length > end); neither parseContentRange() nor executePartialPut() nor doPut() checks that the target resource already exists, that the request is not being used to plant a new file, or that the written path is anything other than 'under the (writable) web application mount'. allowPartialPut defaults to true and DirResourceSet.write()/StandardRoot.write() only check isPathMounted() and read-only state. As a result, when the default servlet is write-enabled (default is read-only, but `readonly=false` is a documented configuration, e.g. for WebDAV/PUT use), a remote client can create arbitrary webapp files, including zero-filled files of attacker-chosen length with attacker-chosen prefix content.
candidate_impact: Arbitrary file creation/overwrite inside the web application resource tree once write is enabled: content injection/defacement, corruption of existing resources, and - where the written location is later consumed by Tomcat or the application (session persistence with deserialization, resource/class loading, JSP/static serving) - a path to remote code execution or session hijacking. Partial PUT also lets the attacker choose the resulting file length and offset, which can be used to craft binary file formats (e.g. serialized objects) precisely. Under the default read-only configuration the servlet returns 405 and the path is not reachable.

candidate_title: RewriteValve decodes the rewritten path after normalising it, so the decoded URI handed to the mapper can retain dot-segments (normalisation invariant violated in CoyoteAdapter's char-type branch)
candidate_root_cause: In RewriteValve.invoke() the rewritten path is normalised while still percent-encoded (RequestUtil.normalize(urlStringRewriteEncoded), line 558) and only afterwards URL-decoded (URLDecoder.decode(urlStringRewriteEncoded, uriCharset), line 565). Any %2e/%2f sequences present in the rewrite output therefore become '.', '..' and '/' only after normalisation. The valve then re-enters CoyoteAdapter.postParseRequest via prepare(); because requestURI()/decodedURI() were set as chars, the char/String branch runs (CoyoteAdapter.java:653-667) and, per its own comment, assumes decodedURI is already 'decoded and normalized' and only calls decodedURI.toChars(). No further normalisation is applied before Mapper.map() (CoyoteAdapter.java:695-697), so mappingData.requestPath, servletPath/pathInfo (and hence getRelativePath() in Default/WebdavServlet and getRequestPathMB() in StandardContextValve) can be derived from a denormalised path.
candidate_impact: Potential access to resources outside the intended request path (information disclosure), bypass of the /WEB-INF and /META-INF direct-access restrictions in StandardContextValve, and, when a write-enabled default servlet/WebDAV is present, potential creation/modification of files outside the intended path. Because StandardRoot.validate() and AbstractFileResourceSet.file() perform their own normalisation and canonical-path containment checks, the practical impact is bounded by whether the denormalised segments survive to those layers; I could not demonstrate end-to-end traversal from source alone.

candidate_title: Open Test Reporting listener executes git in the JVM working directory and copies repository metadata (origin URL, status) into report artifacts
candidate_root_cause: OpenTestReportGeneratingListener.addGitInfo() runs `git` (hardcoded subcommands) through ProcessBuilder without an absolute executable path, with the child working directory set to the JVM's current directory (workingDir = Paths.get(".").toAbsolutePath()). Repository metadata obtained this way is inserted into the Open Test Reporting XML document without sanitization or redaction: `git config --get remote.origin.url` -> repository.withOriginUrl(gitUrl), plus branch, HEAD commit and the full `git status --porcelain` output; the document is written to <outputDir>/open-test-report.xml, which CI/build tooling archives and publishes.
candidate_impact: (1) Local code-execution surface: `git status --porcelain` is executed inside the working directory and therefore processes repository-local configuration; Git features such as `core.fsmonitor` cause Git to spawn a configured helper program, so JUnit can end up executing code chosen by whoever controls that repository state. (2) Information disclosure: the repository's origin URL (frequently `https://user:TOKEN@host/...` in CI), HEAD commit, branch and the full dirty-file listing are written unredacted into a report file that is typically uploaded as a CI artifact or published with test reports, exposing credentials/repository details to anyone who can read the artifact. (3) Robustness/DoS: `exec` reads stdout to EOF before stderr, so a child that blocks on stderr (large output) hangs the reader past the intended 10-second `waitFor` timeout, and process-start failures are rethrown as UncheckedIOException from a listener callback.

candidate_title: jans-config-api does not enforce the CONFIG_API external authorization script decision (broken access control)
candidate_root_cause: In OpenIdAuthorizationService.processAuthorization() the result of externalAuthorization(token, issuer, method, path) is assigned to the local variable `boolean isAuthorized` (line 115), only logged (line 116), and then discarded: the method returns the access token (line 118) with no `if (!isAuthorized) throw ...` enforcement. Its downstream collaborators only return/aggregate a boolean and never abort: ExternalInterceptionService.authorization() propagates ExternalConfigService.checkAuthorization(), which ANDs ConfigApiType.authorize() per script and returns false on denial. The only caller, AuthorizationFilter.filter(), wraps processAuthorization() in try/catch and aborts the request only when an exception is thrown (lines 84-96), so a script's `false` (deny) verdict is functionally ignored. In the JWT access-token branch the external authorization is not even invoked (return at line 92).
candidate_impact: Broken access control on the Config API: requests that a deployment's configured custom authorization policy explicitly denies are still authorized, defeating the documented CONFIG_API interception control (e.g., per-method/path/tenant/IP restrictions encoded in the script). Because only OAuth scopes are still enforced, any client holding a token with the required scopes can perform administrative Config API operations (clients, scopes, attributes, scripts, configuration) that the script intended to block; JWT access tokens bypass the control entirely. The pattern of a computed-but-unused authorization boolean is strong source evidence that an enforcement branch is absent.

candidate_title: Unhardened StAX XMLInputFactory in network/CIM importers enables XXE on untrusted files
candidate_root_cause: Multiple production XML parsers instantiate `XMLInputFactory.newInstance()`/`newFactory()` with JDK defaults and never disable DTD processing or external entity resolution. `javax.xml.stream.supportDTD` and `javax.xml.stream.isSupportingExternalEntities` default to true in the JDK StAX implementation, so a DOCTYPE with internal/external entities in an imported file is processed and resolved. candidate_title: Incorrect loop increment in HTTP/2 PushBuilder percent-decoding corrupts pushed request decoded paths
candidate_root_cause: In ApplicationPushBuilder.decodePercentSequence, the byte array is sized one element per percent-triple (sequence.length()/3) but the loop advances i by 3, indexing bytes[i], while reading source characters at offsets 1 + 3*i and 2 + 3*i. candidate_title: WHATWG URL parser skips IDN/punycode validation for ASCII hosts due to broken "xn--" fast-path check
candidate_root_cause: `WhatWgUrlParser.domainToAscii` implements the WHATWG "domain to ASCII" optimization incorrectly. Per spec (and the method's own comment at lines 285-287), the shortcut of simply lowercasing the domain is only valid when strictly splitting the domain on '.' does not produce ANY label starting with a case-insensitive "xn--". The implementation (lines 288-310) instead: (a) starts scanning at the first '.' (domain.indexOf('.') at line 289), so the first label is never examined at all, and (b) compares the fourth character against '_' (underscore, 0x5F) instead of '-' (hyphen, 0x2D) at line 300, i.e. it tests for "xn-_" rather than "xn--". As a result the condition is effectively never true for real punycode labels and ASCII hostnames containing xn-- labels are returned lower-cased without ever running `IDN.toASCII` (lines 311-328), so malformed/invalid punycode or otherwise IDN-invalid host names that WHATWG/browsers and `IDN.toASCII` reject are accepted by this parser.
candidate_impact: Validation-bypass/laxity in a parser documented as implementing the WHATWG URL Living Standard used by browsers: host names whose punycode (`xn--`) labels are malformed and that `IDN.toASCII`/WHATWG parsing would reject (spec failure) are accepted and normalized only by lowercasing. Applications using ParserType.WHAT_WG for URL acceptance or host allow/deny decisions can therefore base a security decision on a host the spec says is invalid, and the parser's output no longer matches browser/WHATWG canonicalization, enabling divergent interpretation between the validating parser and other components (a known precondition for SSRF/open-redirect/allowlist bypasses). I did not establish a concrete attacker-controlled mapping from an accepted malformed host to a different hostname, so this is reported as a source-evidenced validation weakness, not a confirmed exploit.

Because the parsed content is echoed, the impact is exfiltration rather than blind.

candidate_title: jwt-headers authentication filter grants roles from an unvalidated HTTP header, allowing escalation to GeoServer administrator
candidate_root_cause: In the jwt-headers authentication extension the *username* token is cryptographically validated, but the *roles* are read from a different header and parsed without any signature/expiry/audience verification. `GeoServerJwtHeadersFilter.getPreAuthenticatedPrincipalName` (lines 152-173) calls `tokenValidator.validate(headerValue)` only on the username header and then marks the request; `GeoServerJwtHeadersFilter.getRoles` (lines 179-197) subsequently reads `rolesHeaderName` and hands it to `JwtHeadersRolesExtractor.getRoles` (lines 40-72), which calls `JWSObject.parse(...).getPayload().toJSONObject()` and never calls `verify()` — the only JWS verifier in the module (`TokenSignatureValidator`) is used exclusively for the username token. Extracted role names become `GeoServerRole` authorities directly (line 193) and `RoleConverter.convert` (lines 35-49) passes through any role name that is not in the mapping when `onlyExternalListedRoles` is false (the Java default). Compounding this, all validation switches in `JwtConfiguration` (lines 36-52: `validateToken`, `validateTokenSignature`, `validateTokenExpiry`, …) default to false and `GeoServerJwtHeadersFilterConfigValidator.validateGeoServerJwtHeadersFilterConfig` (lines 44-51) is an empty `// todo`, so a filter can be installed with role extraction enabled and token validation enabled for the username while the roles header is still attacker-controlled.
candidate_impact: Privilege escalation from any authenticated IdP/SSO user (or any requester when token validation is off, which is the configuration default) to GeoServer administrator: the attacker can manage users/roles (`/rest/security/...`), change security rules, read/modify the catalog, and generally gain full control of the server. Because roles are not tied to the signed token, the classic 'only trust the proxy' assumption is violated by the module's own design, which otherwise does verify the username token.
