candidate_title: Guest (unauthenticated) requests are elevated to the application identity for GET /v1/_permissions/* and can read the app's resource-permission table
candidate_root_cause: RestAuthFilter.hasPermission() returns true unconditionally when the extracted resource path matches "^_permissions/.+" and the method is GET, *before* the subject (guest) permission check `parentApp.isAllowedTo(subjectid, resourcePath, method)` is performed. The bypass was apparently intended only for the permission *check* call used by clients (`pc.isAllowed()`, i.e. GET /v1/_permissions/{subjectid}/{base64path}/{method}), but the regex also covers the permission *read* route (GET /v1/_permissions/{subjectid}), which returns the stored ACL for a subject.
candidate_impact: Unauthenticated disclosure of an application's authorization table (subject ids, resource paths and allowed methods, including the wildcard "*" subject and guest "?" grants) and a permission-check oracle for arbitrary subject/resource/method combinations. It also breaks the guest trust boundary in the security model: a self-declared "Anonymous" request is upgraded to the application principal, and any other GET handler reachable under `_permissions/*` (including ones added by custom plugins/handlers) would inherit that identity. The subject-id entries also aid account/resource enumeration for follow-up attacks. Data modification is not reachable through this bypass because it requires the GET method.

candidate_title: Unsigned id_token claims trusted in generic OAuth2 login (POST /jwt_auth) allow account takeover
candidate_root_cause: GenericOAuth2Filter.fetchProfileFromIDP() decodes the payload of a caller-supplied id_token with Utils.base64dec()/Jackson and merges its claims into the user profile without verifying the JWS signature, issuer, audience, expiry or nonce (lines 303-308). candidate_impact: Authentication bypass/account takeover: an unauthenticated attacker can obtain a valid Para JWT for an existing user of any non-root app (if the victim's OAuth2 sub is known, or the victim's email when search is enabled), and can also create arbitrary users with attacker-chosen identity fields (identifier, email, name, picture) that are then trusted by account-linking logic. candidate_title: StarRocks sink/data-node JDBC URL bypasses MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils, enabling JDBC URL attack (local file read / possible deserialization RCE)
candidate_root_cause: The project maintains MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils.filterSensitive() to strip/neutralize MySQL Connector/J properties that enable the classic JDBC connection-URL attack (autoDeserialize, allowLoadLocalInfile, allowUrlInLocalInfile, allowLoadLocalInfileInPath), and applies it to MySQL sink URLs (MySQLSinkDTO.getFromRequest) and to MySQL/StarRocks data-node test connections (StarRocksDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcUrl). The StarRocks sink and StarRocks resource-creation paths never call that filter: the user-supplied jdbcUrl is copied verbatim into stream_sink.ext_params (StarRocksSinkDTO.getFromRequest), a raw data-node URL is copied verbatim in StarRocksSinkOperator.getFromEntity / StarRocksResourceOperator.getStarRocksInfo, and the value is then handed to DriverManager.getConnection(url, ...) with com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver (StarRocksJdbcUtils.getConnection). The same unfiltered URL is also emitted into the sort config (StarRocksProvider -> StarRocksLoadNode.tableOptions() jdbc-url) and consumed by the sort StarRocks connector via StarRocksJdbcConnectionProvider, so the MySQL driver in the sort cluster parses the attacker properties as well. UrlVerificationUtils.extractHostAndValidatePortFromJdbcUrl only checks the host:port shape and does not remove these properties, and StarRocksSinkRequest only rejects whitespace in the URL.
candidate_impact: Server-side connections to an attacker-chosen MySQL-protocol endpoint with attacker-chosen MySQL Connector/J properties. With allowLoadLocalInfile/allowUrlInLocalInfile, the malicious server can request local files and receive their contents (arbitrary file read/exfiltration from the manager and sort hosts, e.g. credentials/configs). With autoDeserialize=true, Connector/J deserializes server-provided data during result handling, which is the well-known JDBC deserialization attack that can lead to remote code execution when a usable gadget chain is on the classpath. The project itself classifies these parameters as security-sensitive, which is why MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils exists.

candidate_root_cause: The project's anti-'JDBC URL attack' control `MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils.filterSensitive` (autoDeserialize / allowLoadLocalInfile / allowUrlInLocalInfile / allowLoadLocalInfileInPath) is only wired into MySQLSinkDTO.getFromRequest, MySQLDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcurl and StarRocksDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcUrl. `StarRocksSinkDTO.getFromRequest` copies the request `jdbcUrl` verbatim, and `OceanBaseSinkDTO.getFromRequest` does the same even though its own Javadoc says 'The config here will be saved to the database, so filter sensitive params before saving'. candidate_impact: Attacker-influenced JDBC URL parameters are consumed inside the manager JVM by MySQL-family drivers. This is the same class of issue the existing filter was written to stop (see the linked jdbc-connection-url-attack reference in JdbcUrlFilter/Constants): untrusted deserialization / arbitrary class instantiation on connect (autoDeserialize, queryInterceptors, socketFactory, propertiesTransform), arbitrary local file read through the LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE family, and SSRF from the manager's network position to internal MySQL/OceanBase services. In a manager compromise the result can be remote code execution on the manager host; at minimum it is a manager-side SSRF/local-file-read primitive available to a low-privileged tenant user.

candidate_title: Java DSL basic authentication is not enforced: authenticateBasicAsync(...).optional discards the authentication result
candidate_root_cause: In AkkaManagement.prepareCombinedRoutes, the javadsl authenticator branch builds Akka HTTP's authenticateBasicAsync directive and then calls `.optional` before `.apply(_ => inner)`. `AuthenticationDirective.optional` turns both CredentialsMissing and CredentialsRejected results into a provided `None` instead of rejecting with AuthenticationFailedRejection, and the resulting Option is thrown away by `_ => inner`. Consequently the inner management routes are always executed, whether or not the Java authenticator supplied by withAuth returns a principal. The scaladsl branch, by contrast, calls `authenticateBasicAsync[...](_ => inner)` and does reject unauthenticated requests, so the two documented APIs have different security semantics.
candidate_impact: Authentication bypass / broken access control on the management HTTP endpoint for Java-DSL deployments. Read endpoints (cluster members/leader detail, shard stats, health state, bootstrap seed nodes) become readable without credentials despite configured auth, and when `route-providers-read-only=false` an unauthenticated attacker can leave/down cluster members, force the node to join an attacker-supplied address, prepare a full cluster shutdown, and change/disable log levels (documented DoS vector). This defeats the operator's intended mitigation against the documented risks of the unsecured management endpoint.

candidate_title: Java DSL basic authentication for Akka Management routes is never enforced (authentication directive result discarded)
candidate_root_cause: In `wrapWithAuthenticatorIfPresent`, the `(None, Some(auth))` branch wraps the basic-auth directive with `.optional` and then ignores the directive value (`_ => inner`). `optional` converts authentication failure (missing/rejected credentials) into `None` instead of a 401 rejection, so the inner route (all registered management routes) executes unconditionally. The user-supplied Java authenticator's returned `Optional<String>` is never inspected, so `Optional.empty()` (invalid/no credentials) cannot cause a rejection. The analogous Scala DSL branch (line 191-192) correctly uses `authenticateBasicAsync(...)(_ => inner)` and does enforce authentication, showing this is an asymmetric defect rather than a repository-wide design choice.
candidate_impact: Authentication bypass: management endpoints that an operator believes are protected by Java-DSL basic authentication accept unauthenticated requests. The endpoint is unauthenticated only in deployments using the Java DSL auth feature; the Scala DSL and no-auth configurations behave as before.

candidate_title: Authorization rules rendered unreachable by a catch-all `/**` permitAll matcher registered first in SecurityConfig
candidate_root_cause: In `SecurityConfig.filterChain(HttpSecurity)` the authorization rules are added through three separate `authorizeHttpRequests(...)` calls on the same `AuthorizationManagerRequestMatcherRegistry`, which accumulates mappings in insertion order (`RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager` returns the decision of the first matching mapping). Line 99 registers `requestMatchers("/**").permitAll()` before the `IgnoredRequestMatcher` and `RestRequestMatcher.INSTANCE.authenticated()` rules (lines 100-101) and before `parseProtectedResources(http, protectedResources)` (line 103, rule creation at lines 140-179). Because `/**` matches every request, the `authenticated()` requirement and every `hasAnyRole(...)` rule built from `para.security.protected` are dead code: requests that are supposed to require authentication/roles are permitted anonymously. The catch-all rule should be registered after (or instead of) the specific rules.
candidate_impact: Silent loss of authentication/role enforcement for any resource the operator marked protected through Spring Security: unauthenticated/unauthorized access to protected pages or endpoints (information disclosure, privileged functionality exposure), and a false sense of security because the feature is documented and seems configured. The API itself retains the plugin's custom signature/JWT checks (`RestAuthFilter`), which limits the blast radius for `/v1/*`.

candidate_title: BeanMap exposes the suppressed class property and enables class-loader path traversal
candidate_root_cause: BeanMap.initialize() obtains property descriptors with the raw JDK Introspector and unconditionally stores every readable property, including the synthetic "class" property backed by Object.getClass(). It never consults SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector, unlike PropertyUtilsBean, whose resetBeanIntrospectors() installs SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector.SUPPRESS_CLASS by default. Because BeanMap also implements Map, PropertyUtilsBean.getNestedProperty()/BeanUtilsBean.setProperty() treat it as a dynamic map and resolve attacker-supplied keys such as "class" directly through BeanMap.get(), bypassing the normal JavaBean introspection path where "class" is suppressed.
candidate_impact: Bypasses the default suppression of the class property, disclosing Class and ClassLoader objects and potentially allowing traversal or modification of class-loader state. In applications with a suitable object graph and writable properties, this is the CVE-2014-0114-style class-loader manipulation pattern and can lead to remote code execution or container compromise; where no writable chain is reachable, it is at least a sensitive class/class-loader disclosure and an access-control bypass.

candidate_root_cause: The default mitigation against class-level property access is implemented only inside PropertyUtilsBean's introspection/descriptor machinery (DefaultBeanIntrospector + SuppressPropertiesBeanIntrospector.SUPPRESS_CLASS, PropertyUtilsBean.java 1200-1204). candidate_title: SpEL injection in dashboard/widget query condition (QueryCondition) evaluated from configured queryValue
candidate_root_cause: QueryCondition.queryValue is used to build a SpEL expression with only a weak substring gate (`queryValueIsDateTimeSpelExpression`, QueryCondition.kt:82-86: value must start with `${`, end with `}`, and contain the literal text `localDateTimeNow`). The substring check can be satisfied by attacker-chosen text, after which the text between the first `${` and the first `}` is parsed by `SpelExpressionParser` and evaluated through `StandardEvaluationContext` (QueryCondition.kt:94-107). The evaluation context restricts neither type references (`T(...)`) nor method invocation and uses only the default type locator, so `java.lang` classes (e.g. Runtime/ProcessBuilder) remain reachable. There is no allowlist that the expression is exactly the intended `localDateTimeNow` variable.
candidate_impact: Remote code execution with the application's privileges (JVM/OS command execution via java.lang.Runtime/ProcessBuilder type references), plus disclosure/tampering of data the application can reach. Because the expression is persisted in widget configuration, it is stored rather than reflected, and it is re-executed each time the affected widget data is requested. With the default deployment the entry point is an administrative configuration API, so the immediate privilege boundary is admin-to-OS within the Valtimo application; where the management API or dashboard configuration is exposed to less-trusted operators/configurations, the boundary is lower.

candidate_title: StarRocks sink/data-node JDBC URL skips MySQL sensitive-parameter filtering, letting attacker-controlled autoDeserialize reach MySQL Connector/J (untrusted deserialization in Manager)
candidate_root_cause: The project centrally mitigates JDBC-URL parameter attacks with MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils.filterSensitive() (strips/forces autoDeserialize, allowLoadLocalInfile, allowUrlInLocalInfile, allowLoadLocalInfileInPath; handles URL-encoding/whitespace). MySQL and OceanBase paths apply it (MySQLSinkDTO.getFromRequest line 88 with the explicit @apiNote "filter sensitive params before saving", MySQLResourceOperator line 137, OceanBaseJdbcUtils line 80, MySQLDataNodeDTO line 84, StarRocksDataNodeDTO line 75). The StarRocks sink path does not: StarRocksSinkDTO.getFromRequest copies request.getJdbcUrl() verbatim; StarRocksResourceOperator.getStarRocksInfo() and StarRocksSinkOperator.getFromEntity() assign dataNodeInfo.getUrl() raw; and StarRocksJdbcUtils.getConnection() performs only a prefix/host/port format check (UrlVerificationUtils) before Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") + DriverManager.getConnection(url,...). The only request-side validation is @Pattern("^((?!\\s).)*$") on StarRocksSinkRequest.jdbcUrl. Since the prefix accepted is literally 'jdbc:mysql://' (StarRocksJdbcUtils line 42), extra query parameters such as autoDeserialize=true, queryInterceptors=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.interceptors.ServerStatusDiffInterceptor, allowLoadLocalInfile=true, allowUrlInLocalInfile=true pass validation untouched.
candidate_impact: Untrusted Java deserialization driven by a remote party inside the Manager process (potential RCE depending on gadget availability), arbitrary local file disclosure from the Manager host via Connector/J allowLoadLocalInfile/allowUrlInLocalInfile, and SSRF/port-scan of internal hosts as the Manager. candidate_title: Unauthenticated OpenAPI login creates a default-admin Shiro session that is accepted by the Manager web APIs
candidate_root_cause: The manager uses a single Shiro SecurityManager/session for two different authentication surfaces. `/openapi/**` is handled by OpenAPIFilter, which (with the shipped default `openapi.auth.enabled=false`) logs the request in with an empty SecretToken; OpenAPIAuthenticatingRealm.doDefaultAuth then authenticates the built-in `admin` account and grants it INLONG_ADMIN/INLONG_OPERATOR/TENANT_ADMIN/TENANT_OPERATOR. Shiro persists the authenticated subject in the HTTP session (default DefaultSubjectDAO/session storage enabled), and the web chain's gate (AuthenticationFilter on `/**`) only checks `subject.isAuthenticated()` without verifying which realm produced the session. Consequently the openapi-created session is reused for `/api/**`, and role checks are resolved from that principal by WebAuthorizingRealm.
candidate_impact: Full compromise of the InLong Manager control plane from an unauthenticated network position: create/modify/delete users (including changing other users' passwords/account types, giving persistent takeover), clusters, cluster nodes with SSH credentials, data nodes, groups/streams/sinks and SaaS modules. Agent-installer flows and module install/start/stop commands are driven by these records, so the bypass can also lead to arbitrary command execution on managed agent hosts (ExcuteLinux.exeCmd on the installer) when the attacker updates/assigns modules; tenant isolation is also defeated because the principal is the global admin.

candidate_title: Pre-authentication pipeTransfer (V2 COMBINE) instantiates attacker-chosen classes and deserializes attacker bytes; pipeSubscribe likewise unauthenticated
candidate_root_cause: Unlike every other method in the same class, `ClientRPCServiceImpl.pipeTransfer` and `pipeSubscribe` do not invoke `SESSION_MANAGER.checkLogin(...)`, so the pipe-transfer and subscription receivers are reachable by any network client without a session. For version-2 pipe requests, `IoTDBReceiverAgent.receive` routes directly to `TwoStageAggregateReceiver` (which has no handshake case and requires no credentials - the internal `TwoStageAggregateSender` also never logs in). Parsing `CombineRequest` then reads a fully attacker-controlled class name from the wire body and performs `state = (State) Class.forName(stateClassName).newInstance(); state.deserialize(transferReq.body);` with no allow-list or type whitelist.
candidate_impact: Pre-authentication, remote attacker can force the DataNode to load and instantiate arbitrary classes present on the classpath (executing static initializers and no-arg constructors) and to invoke `State.deserialize` on any class implementing that interface with attacker-controlled bytes. Because authentication is missing at the entry point, the intended trust boundary (an authenticated internal peer driving the two-stage exchange) is not enforced, and the same omission lets an unauthenticated client handshake with the subscription receiver and poll subscribed topic data (information disclosure).

candidate_title: HTTP/2 client trusts server-supplied PUSH_PROMISE stream IDs and pushed authority without validation
candidate_root_cause: On the client side, HTTP2ClientSession.onPushPromise (HTTP2ClientSession.java:98-127) accepts the `promisedStreamId` carried in a server PUSH_PROMISE frame with no RFC 9113 §6.6 validation: it does not require the promised ID to be even (server-initiated), strictly greater than all previously promised IDs, or not already consumed/closed, and it does not check that the associated stream is a valid open client stream. candidate_title: Markdown output escaping crashes / mis-escapes on reserved characters (one-char regex match indexed as two, mismatched output offsets)
candidate_root_cause: In MarkdownEscapeHandler, RESERVED_CHARS_PATTERN lists single-character alternatives before the two-character ones ("(?<!\\\\)\\*|(?<!\\\\)\\*\\*|(?<!\\\\)__|(?<!\\\\)_|(?<!\\\\)`"), and Java regex alternation is leftmost-first, so a '*', '_' or '`' match has length 1; the replacement expression however unconditionally uses matcher.group().charAt(0) AND matcher.group().charAt(1), which throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException for any length-1 match. Independently, the loop offset 'i' is advanced by (matcher.end()-matcher.start()+1) while the buffer grows by only (replacementLength-matchLength) per replacement, so for more than one match the start/end indexes used by StringBuffer.replace drift into the wrong positions (corrupt/missed escaping, further exceptions). MarkdownEscapeWikiPrinter.flush() invokes escape() on every non-empty buffer, so all renderer output text (bold '**', monospace '`', code-macro backticks, list/quote/table cell text, link labels) flows through this code.
candidate_impact: Denial of the Markdown rendering/conversion path (RuntimeException aborts rendering of any content containing reserved characters) and incorrect escaping of reserved characters in produced Markdown (characters that should be backslash-escaped can be left active or corrupted), i.e. output-integrity/availability impact rather than demonstrated code execution. Not demonstrated to be remotely triggerable in a default deployment: it depends on which XWiki feature invokes the Markdown renderer.

candidate_title: OAuth2 'external' grant type issues tokens for arbitrary users without credential verification
candidate_root_cause: `ExternalOAuthTokenGranter` both implements `OAuthTokenIssuer` and extends `AbstractTokenGranter` for grant type "external", and is declared as a Spring bean in the REST dispatcher/authorization-server context. Spring OAuth2 collects `TokenGranter` beans into the token endpoint's composite granter, and the shipped default client configuration includes `external` in `cuba.rest.client.authorizedGrantTypes`. Unlike the password granter (which delegates to `CubaUserAuthenticationProvider` and verifies credentials), the overridden `getOAuth2Authentication` trusts the request parameters: it takes `username` and `sessionId` straight from `tokenRequest.getRequestParameters()`, only null-checks them, and then wraps them in an `ExternalAuthenticationToken` that is marked authenticated. No password, LDAP bind, client-side password check, or ownership check of `sessionId` is performed. The stored token therefore binds an attacker-chosen login to the token, and `ClientProxyTokenStore.processSession` will perform a trusted-client login (using the server-side `cuba.trustedClientPassword`) for that login when the session is absent/unknown, yielding a real session for the victim user.
candidate_impact: Authentication bypass and privilege escalation: an attacker with REST client credentials can mint valid access/refresh tokens for arbitrary users, including administrators, without knowing their passwords or possessing a valid session. This yields full REST API access (entity read/update/delete, exposed service methods, file upload/download, permission and metadata endpoints) under the victim's account, and a refresh token with the configured (default 365-day) lifetime. The affected token remains usable even though no real login ever occurred.

candidate_title: Discarded result of legacy '.crumb' lookup makes CrumbFilter compatibility fallback ineffective
candidate_root_cause: In `CrumbFilter.doFilter`, the crumb is first read from the configured field name. If absent, the comment states a compatibility fallback to the legacy `.crumb` request value is performed, but the call `extractCrumbFromRequest(httpRequest, ".crumb")` at line 139 is a pure no-side-effect call whose result is thrown away (no `crumb = ` assignment). Because `extractCrumbFromRequest` only reads a header/parameter and returns it, the fallback is dead code: `crumb` remains null, `valid` can never become true through that path, and the POST is answered with 403. candidate_title: QuicheSendInfo.getAtNanos reads nsec from tv_sec (wrong struct offset), yielding incorrect send-time-in-nanos
candidate_root_cause: QuicheSendInfo.getAtNanos() is documented to return the quiche_send_info.timespec 'in nanos', so it must combine tv_sec (seconds) with tv_nsec (nanoseconds). Both reads use QUICHE_SEND_INFO_OFFSETOF_AT + TIMESPEC_OFFSETOF_TV_SEC: sec = getPrimitiveValue(..., TIMESPEC_OFFSETOF_TV_SEC, SIZEOF_TIME_T) and nsec = getPrimitiveValue(..., TIMESPEC_OFFSETOF_TV_SEC, SIZEOF_LONG). The second read should use TIMESPEC_OFFSETOF_TV_NSEC (which is defined in Quiche.java but is never referenced anywhere in the repository, showing the intended use site was lost/modified). The returned value is therefore SECONDS.toNanos(tv_sec) + tv_sec instead of SECONDS.toNanos(tv_sec) + tv_nsec.
candidate_impact: Any scheduling/pacing decision that consumes this value (e.g. deciding when a prepared datagram should be handed to the socket) is computed from a wrong absolute time, so packets can be released earlier/later than quiche intended, degrading packet pacing/timer behaviour. I could not demonstrate a concrete remote exploit (no memory-safety consequence, no attacker-controlled data in the computation, and the helper may be dead code in this snapshot), so the security impact is limited/uncertain and is reported as a defect lead rather than a confirmed exploitable vulnerability.

candidate_title: BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches accepts any password sharing the first 72 bytes of the real password (bcrypt truncation not enforced)
candidate_root_cause: BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode and matches (crypto/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/crypto/bcrypt/BCryptPasswordEncoder.java lines 104-111 and 121-134) never enforce bcrypt's 72-byte input limit before calling BCrypt.hashpw/BCrypt.checkpw. candidate_impact: Authentication bypass / credential confusion for long passwords: authentication succeeds for a password that is not the enrolled password as long as its first 72 bytes match. candidate_title: BCryptPasswordEncoder/BCrypt silently ignore password bytes after the 72nd, so distinct long passwords compare as equal
candidate_root_cause: The Blowfish key schedule consumes exactly 18 32-bit words (72 bytes) of the password: BCrypt.key() iterates i < this.P.length (=18) calling streamtoword() (BCrypt.java:416-429) and BCrypt.ekskey() does the same (BCrypt.java:452-464); streamtowords() advances modulo data.length (BCrypt.java:366-373), so only password bytes 0-71 can ever influence the state. Neither the public hashpw/checkpw entry points (BCrypt.java:588-604, 762-776) nor BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode/matches (BCryptPasswordEncoder.java:105-111, 121-134) check rawPassword/encoded length, warn, or reject inputs longer than 72 bytes; matches() simply recomputes the hash of the candidate and compares it (line 133). candidate_title: BCryptPasswordEncoder/BCrypt do not enforce bcrypt's 72-byte maximum password length
candidate_root_cause: BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode(CharSequence) and matches(CharSequence,String) forward the raw password unconditionally to BCrypt.hashpw/BCrypt.checkpw, and the underlying BCrypt.hashpw(String,String)/hashpw(byte[],String)/hashpw(byte[],String,boolean) routines contain no check that the UTF-8 password is at most 72 bytes. bcrypt ("$2a/$2b/$2y") defines 72 bytes as the maximum effective password length and widely used implementations truncate input at that boundary. This implementation instead cycles the complete byte array through the Blowfish key schedule (streamtowords: `off = (off + 1) % data.length`), so a >72-byte password yields a hash that neither matches a spec-compliant/truncating bcrypt hash nor is truncated consistently.
candidate_impact: Credential validation flaw: passwords longer than bcrypt's 72-byte limit are silently accepted and handled non-spec-compliantly. In any environment where a truncating bcrypt implementation participates in verification, a supplied password that differs from the real password only after byte 72 authenticates successfully; in a pure-Spring deployment the stored hash becomes non-interoperable with other bcrypt implementations (and vice versa), which can also be abused during hash migration/verification gaps. Effectively, entropy/semantics beyond 72 bytes are undefined, weakening the guarantee that the full user password guards the account.

candidate_title: Authenticated client can register an arbitrary WorkSpace and inject WorkBundle file paths, giving SSRF plus arbitrary file read/move on FilePickUpClient nodes
candidate_root_cause: The cluster work-distribution protocol does not validate trust inputs on either side. `WorkSpaceClientOpenWorkSpaceAction.openTheSpace` takes a caller-supplied `workSpaceName`, sanitizes only CR/LF (`RequestUtil.sanitizeParameter`), and calls `PickUpSpace.openSpace(spaceName)` after a namespace lookup of the caller-supplied client place name. `PickUpSpace.take()` then builds an outbound HTTP request URL directly from that string (`KeyManipulator.getServiceHostUrl(space)`) and treats the returned XML as a `WorkBundle`. `WorkBundle.buildWorkBundle` stores `outputRoot`, `eatPrefix`, `simpleMode` and each `workFileName` verbatim, and `FilePickUpClient.processBundle` opens/reads the attacker-supplied paths and uses those strings for rename destinations via `PickUpPlace.getInProcessFileNameFor` / `renameToInProcessAreaAs` (`holdingArea + "/" + base`, no canonicalization) and `renameFileToDoneArea` (`outputRoot + "/" + base`). candidate_title: Uncontrolled self-recursion in ASN1ByteChannelReader typed octet-string decoders (potential StackOverflowError DoS)
candidate_root_cause: In opendj-server-legacy/src/main/java/org/opends/server/protocols/ldap/ASN1ByteChannelReader.java the class is a thin delegating wrapper around an org.forgerock.opendj.io.ASN1Reader (field 'reader'): every method delegates via reader.<same method>(...). Three methods instead invoke themselves with identical signatures and no receiver, so they recurse unconditionally: readOctetString(byte type) -> readOctetString(type) (line 444); readOctetString(byte type, ByteStringBuilder builder) -> readOctetString(type, builder) (line 454); readOctetStringAsString(byte type) -> readOctetStringAsString(type) (line 464). The correct bodies are reader.readOctetString(type), reader.readOctetString(type, builder) and reader.readOctetStringAsString(type), matching the other overloads (e.g. lines 438-440, 448-450, 458-460).
candidate_impact: Availability/denial of service on the LDAP listener: an uncaught StackOverflowError in a request-decoding path can kill the request-handler/worker thread or repeatedly drop client connections, and the StackOverflowError can leave the request handler loop in a failed state. It also violates the public ASN1Reader contract, so any server extension, embedded usage, or future protocol feature that uses the typed API on the wire reader fails closed on arbitrary requests rather than decoding them. No data disclosure, authentication bypass, or code execution follows from the recursion itself; impact is availability and robustness.

candidate_title: Path traversal in OAuth2 file-based access-token resolver via attacker-controlled Bearer token
candidate_root_cause: FileAccessTokenResolver.resolve() treats the client-supplied OAuth2 access token as a file name and concatenates it into a path with no confinement check: `new File(folderPath, token)` followed by `new FileInputStream(...)` (lines 49-55). Java's File(parent, child) strips leading separators from an absolute child but does not canonicalise or reject `..` components, so a token such as `../../../../<path>` escapes the configured `ds-cfg-oauth2-access-token-directory`. The file content is parsed as JSON and drives the resulting AccessTokenInfo: `scope`, `expireTime` and the authzid JSON pointer value that Authorization.createSecurityContextInjectionFilter() turns into `u:<value>` / `dn:<value>` in the SecurityContext, which server-legacy's InternalProxyAuthzFilter then resolves to an LDAP entry and uses as the authenticated identity for the request.
candidate_impact: Filesystem path traversal from an HTTP-controlled string: the server opens and JSON-parses a file of the attacker's choosing outside the intended token directory (arbitrary file read is constrained to JSON-parseable content because of `Json.readJsonLenient`). When a suitable JSON file is available, the attacker-supplied file fully defines the request identity, scope set and expiry, so the request can be authenticated as an arbitrary identity resolvable by the configuration's IdentityMapper (e.g. `uid=<victim>`), i.e. authentication bypass/impersonation against the REST/LDAP gateway. Proxy-Authorization/PROXIED_AUTH checks on the internal connection remain in place at the server, so the achievable privilege level depends on that configuration, but the token-directory trust boundary is clearly broken.

candidate_title: Path traversal in solon-web-staticfiles filesystem repositories allows arbitrary file read
candidate_root_cause: StaticResourceHandler takes the request path from ctx.pathNew() and passes it to StaticMappings.find(), which only checks a path-prefix match (path.startsWith(m.pathPrefix)) and then hands the remaining, attacker-controlled relative path to the repository. FileStaticRepository.find()/ExtendStaticRepository.find() do `new File(location, relativePath)` and serve the file if it exists, with no rejection of '.'/'..' segments, no canonicalization, and no check that the resolved file stays under the repository root. WebContextBase.path() only collapses duplicate '/' characters (Utils.trimDuplicates) and never resolves dot segments, so a raw request path such as `/mapped/../../../../opt/app/config.properties` survives intact when Solon's own lightweight servers are used.
candidate_impact: Arbitrary file read within the permissions of the application process: configuration files with credentials/keys, environment files, source artifacts adjacent to the static root, etc. This is a direct confidentiality breach that can enable further compromise (e.g., reading datasource/JWT/vault secrets). It is an unauthenticated, network-reachable primitive in deployments using a filesystem static mapping and a non-normalizing server/proxy.

candidate_title: SslHandler.wrapMultiple() can spin the event loop indefinitely when the SSLEngine makes no progress (wrap path)
candidate_root_cause: SslHandler.wrapMultiple(ByteBufAllocator, SSLEngine, ByteBuf, ByteBuf) slices the pending plaintext and calls the low-level wrap(...) in a do/while (in.readableBytes() > 0) loop. It only exits early when the result status is CLOSED or when the output buffer would be too small; there is no check that the engine actually made progress (bytesConsumed/bytesProduced). When the SSLEngine must unwrap first (handshake in progress / NEED_UNWRAP), SSLEngine.wrap returns SSLEngineResult(OK, NEED_UNWRAP, 0, 0). SslHandler then restores in.readerIndex by the unread slice length and loops again with exactly the same input, so the loop never terminates. The sibling unwrap loop at SslHandler.java:1556-1566 does contain the analogous consumed==0 && produced==0 break, so the wrap-side path is missing the same guard. Preconditions: wrapDataSize is configured > MAX_PLAINTEXT_LENGTH (16 KiB) or <= 0 (SslHandler.setWrapDataSize, which is a documented public API), the application has a pending write larger than 16 KiB while the TLS handshake is not yet finished, and the peer keeps the handshake incomplete (e.g., stalls before ServerHello/Finished).
candidate_impact: Unbounded CPU spin inside the channel's EventLoop thread. The event loop cannot service I/O, timers or the SslHandler handshake-timeout task (it is scheduled on the same executor), so the affected connection and every other connection on that event loop hang indefinitely (denial of service) until the JVM/process is restarted; with a default NioEventLoopGroup this can stall many channels sharing the loop. A role holding SELECT/MODIFY on the root data resource ('ALL KEYSPACES') therefore obtains SELECT/MODIFY on system_auth.roles (and other system tables) even though it is not a superuser; nothing in ClientState special-cases replicated/local system keyspaces for DML.

candidate_root_cause: AbstractNio2BlobStore never normalizes or confines the caller-supplied key. candidate_root_cause: DomainServerCredential.verify() compares the managed server's secret token with the token supplied in the attacker-controlled SASL evidence using String.equals(), which returns at the first differing character. candidate_root_cause: `ConfigurationFile.snapshot(String prefix, String comment)` sanitizes only the `comment` via `FilePersistenceUtils.sanitizeFileName(comment)`, which strips path separators and other illegal characters. candidate_title: Element-size check in BaseNDManager.isCompatible compares a value with itself, breaking NDArray buffer/DataType validation (type confusion, native OOB read)
candidate_root_cause: In `api/src/main/java/ai/djl/ndarray/BaseNDManager.java`, `isCompatible(DataType type1, DataType type2)` begins with `if (type1.getNumOfBytes() != type1.getNumOfBytes()) { return false; }` (line 479). Comparing the same expression to itself is always false, so the intended guard that rejects buffers whose element width differs from the target `DataType` never fires. The remaining branches only check the 2-byte special case (`type1` 2 bytes => return true) and format/integer compatibility, so a `ShortBuffer` (always mapped to FLOAT16/2 bytes by `DataType.fromBuffer`) is accepted for *every* target DataType, and narrower same-format/integer buffers (e.g., INT8/INT32) are accepted for wider integer targets. `validateBuffer` (lines 451-476) then only compares element *counts* for non-ByteBuffer inputs (`expectedSize = expected`), so no size check compensates.
candidate_impact: Type confusion: buffers of the wrong element type/size are accepted as valid NDArray data. In the MXNet direct-buffer path this becomes a native out-of-bounds read: heap memory beyond the caller's buffer is copied into an NDArray (potential heap content disclosure if that array is later serialized/returned to a client, and possible JVM/native crash). In non-direct/other-engine paths it produces unhandled `BufferOverflowException`/`ClassCastException` (denial of service) or silently corrupt/misinterpreted tensor data used in inference/training.

candidate_title: SQL injection via unescaped caller-supplied patterns in SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges()
candidate_root_cause: getTablePrivileges() constructs its SQL text by string concatenation and does not neutralize single quotes in the pattern arguments. Line 1989 inserts tableNamePattern verbatim into "... where table_name = '<pattern>'"; lines 1997/1999 insert schemaPattern after unescapeChars(), which only reverses LIKE escapes (\_, \%, \\) and escapes double quotes for identifier contexts (escapeSqlQuotes) -- it never escapes single quotes, even though the value is placed inside a single-quoted string literal. A single quote in either argument therefore terminates the string literal and the rest of the argument is parsed as SQL. Sibling methods in the same class (getTables line 1538, getColumns line 1716, getSchemas line 3297, getProcedures/getFunctions line 1425, getStreams line 2893) do call escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand(), demonstrating the intended neutralization that is missing here.
candidate_impact: SQL injection into the Snowflake session at the driver layer. An attacker able to influence the metadata pattern can alter the WHERE predicate (e.g. defeat the intended table/schema filter), use UNION/expressions to make the query return data from other tables or views readable by the connection role, and -- if server-side multi-statement execution is enabled (MULTI_STATEMENT_COUNT) -- potentially append further statements. The exfiltrated values are surfaced to the application through the getTablePrivileges ResultSet, so authorization decisions or displays built on this API can be bypassed and data disclosed within the session role's rights.

candidate_title: Post-login open redirect via unvalidated `from`/Referer in OicSecurityRealm.getValidRedirectUrl
candidate_root_cause: getValidRedirectUrl() builds `new URL(new URL(rootUrl), url)` and accepts any result whose string starts with rootUrl (`redirectUrl.startsWith(rootUrl)`). For an absolute attacker-supplied URL this check is a pure string-prefix test, so any attacker host whose name continues the rootUrl string (userinfo form `rootUrl` + `@evil.example`, or suffix form `rootUrl` + `.evil.example`) passes when rootUrl does not end with '/'. The validated value is persisted in the HTTP session (SESSION_POST_LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL_KEY) by doCommenceLogin and consumed unchanged by doFinishLogin's `response.sendRedirect(...)`.
candidate_impact: Open redirect after successful authentication: an attacker can direct a freshly authenticated Jenkins user to an attacker-controlled origin that mimics Jenkins. No authentication is required to create the malicious link, and the redirect occurs on the trusted Jenkins origin.

candidate_title: Unvalidated JSONP `_jsonp` callback value is reflected verbatim into an executable JavaScript response
candidate_root_cause: CXF's JSONP support accepts the callback function name from the request query string and never validates it against a safe JavaScript-identifier pattern (or escapes it). JsonpInInterceptor.getCallbackValue() reads `JAXRSUtils.getStructuredParams(queryString, "&", false, false).getFirst(callbackParam)` (callbackParam defaults to `_jsonp`) and stores the raw string under the exchange key `JSONP.CALLBACK`. The output-side interceptors then take that value and write it, unmodified, as the first bytes of the response body: JsonpPreStreamInterceptor writes `callback + "("` and JsonpJaxrsWriterInterceptor writes `callback + "("`, while the content type is forced to `application/x-javascript` (AbstractJsonpOutInterceptor.writeValue writes the string with UTF-8, no encoding). No component in the in/out path checks the value, so `?_jsonp=` can contain arbitrary JavaScript (including parentheses, quotes, `//`, or `</script>`-style HTML).
candidate_impact: Cross-site scripting / script-content injection: an attacker can make victim browsers execute attacker-chosen JavaScript in the context of the origin that serves the JSONP endpoint (the injected callback is treated as code by any consumer that loads the URL as a script, e.g. `<script src="https://victim/app/rest?_jsonp=...">`), enabling session/data theft, CSRF token theft, or acting as a script gadget; where the browser content-sniffs the `application/x-javascript` response as HTML, the injected HTML is rendered directly. At minimum it is uncontrolled reflected script content (CWE-79/CWE-116) that would normally be prevented by a callback-name allow-list.

candidate_title: JavaScript attribute escaping omits `&`, allowing HTML-entity decode to break out of JS string literals in `on*` attributes
candidate_root_cause: `gg.jte.html.escape.Escape.javaScriptAttribute` (jte-runtime/src/main/java/gg/jte/html/escape/Escape.java:66-86, switch at 73-82) escapes `'` (\x27), `"` (\x22), `\`, and control characters, but not `&`. It is selected for every attribute whose name starts with `on` (OwaspHtmlTemplateOutput.java:70-71). Because the emitted value is placed inside an HTML attribute in the response, the browser decodes character references in the attribute value before the event handler is compiled as JavaScript. An attacker value such as `');alert(1);//` therefore becomes a literal `'` in the DOM handler, terminating the template's JS string and injecting statements. In contrast, Escape.htmlAttribute (line 34) and Escape.htmlContent (line 15) do escape `&`; javaScriptBlock (script raw-text bodies) is not affected because character references are not decoded there, which shows the omission is specific to the attribute context.

Requires a plausible but specific template pattern (inline event handler + user data inside a JS string), hence not a universal XSS in every jte app.
